81: Spiking Neural Networks process information through discrete, event-driven spikes and promise energy-efficient artificial intelligence. Yet their software is fragmented: Brian2 for biological modeling, NEST for large-scale simulation, Nengo for neuromorphic deployment, and snnTorch and SpikingJelly for gradient-based training in PyTorch. No published study benchmarks all five on the same hardware, so there is no comparable evidence for choosing between them.
82: This thesis introduces an open benchmarking suite that runs identical leaky integrate-and-fire inference, scalability and MNIST training workloads on five simulators and eleven executable backends, with a web dashboard for exploring the results. Simulation runs on one fixed processor-based platform, so runtime differences reflect the simulator rather than the hardware. Accelerator execution is future work. Every run is kept, with machine, library versions and configuration recorded programmatically.
83: The main contribution is five findings showing that the simulator ordering is not stable. By runtime, the ordering at ten thousand neurons agrees with that at five hundred neurons at only tau = 0.236, and at one hundred neurons at no more than 0.273 in any of four measurement sessions. Orderings re-measured at the same size agree at tau = 0.745 or better. Scaling exponents split configurations into problem-dominated and overhead-dominated regimes. The flattest recompiles on every invocation, so it measures its own compiler rather than the simulation. Memory growth per neuron spans the simulators by over two orders of magnitude, only moderately related to runtime (tau = +0.418). Learning cost per image spans over three orders of magnitude. With processor utilisation measured correctly, the energy proxy tracks an analytic synaptic-operation count for every backend whose runtime follows the workload, and keeps its ordering under substantial constant error. However, it is largely runtime rescaled except where a simulator uses several cores. It estimates joules rather than measuring them, and physical validation is future work.
84: The thesis also releases the benchmark suite and dataset with per-run provenance, an interactive dashboard, an environment probe that finds executable hardware by running a kernel, and a sensitivity analysis separating simulator properties from experimental artefacts. Twelve corrected defects are documented. One was a processor-utilisation instrument that failed in two successive forms; it was replaced and checked against known loads, and the affected experiments re-measured. All three research questions are answered, with the conditions each answer holds under.
222: Biological neurons communicate through short, discrete electrical events called spikes, and most neurons in a living brain are silent most of the time. This sparse, event-driven activity is a main reason biological computation is so energy efficient. Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) follow this principle of discontinuity directly: spiking neurons fire discrete spikes only when their membrane potential crosses a threshold ⟦C1:[1]⟧, instead of exchanging continuous activations. Cost is therefore proportional to input activity rather than nominal model size. SNNs are considered a low-power alternative to conventional deep networks ⟦C2:[1]⟧ and a route to energy-efficient artificial intelligence, especially on neuromorphic hardware. Reported gains are substantial. SpikingJelly trains about eleven-fold faster than conventional implementations ⟦C3:[2]⟧. The Speck chip performs real-time inference at sub-milliwatt power ⟦C4:[3]⟧. Intel’s Loihi 2 runs a complete radar-processing pipeline on real sensor data within an event-driven energy budget conventional hardware cannot match ⟦C5:[4]⟧. Neuromorphic processors have enabled on-board inference within the power envelope of satellites ⟦C6:[5]⟧. Each result is convincing alone. But each used different hardware, workloads and measurement methods, so the figures cannot be compared directly. The field lacks a common quantitative baseline.
223: The size of the field has changed in the last two years, and so has the cost of being unable to compare results across tools. Muir and Sheik ⟦C1:[6]⟧ describe neuromorphic computing as moving from isolated single-chip demonstrations to systems that must succeed commercially. They name the lack of standardized, comparable evaluation across the software stack as one obstacle to that transition. The community has begun to respond. The NeuroBench framework ⟦C2:[7]⟧ was assembled by more than a hundred authors because results from different groups could not be placed on the same axis. It proposes an agreed metric vocabulary for reporting them (Section 2.4). NeuroBench, however, covers algorithms and hardware systems. It does not address the layer this thesis studies: the simulation software a researcher runs on an ordinary processor, long before any neuromorphic device is involved, where tools are actually chosen.
225: This fragmentation extends to the software researchers must use. Five mature, actively maintained simulators exist, each with a different design philosophy. Brian2 offers flexible equation-level modeling for computational neuroscience ⟦C1:[8]⟧. NEST is optimized for very large-scale point-neuron simulation ⟦C2:[9]⟧. Nengo compiles functional specifications onto neuromorphic hardware through the Neural Engineering Framework ⟦C3:[10]⟧ and has built spiking controllers for real robots ⟦C4:[11]⟧. snnTorch embeds spiking models in PyTorch with surrogate-gradient training ⟦C5:[12]⟧, and SpikingJelly takes the same tensor-based approach, focusing on training throughput ⟦C6:[2]⟧. All five are widely used and well documented, but each is tuned for a different purpose. A researcher starting a project has no objective, reproducible way to decide which fits a given workload and hardware. Selection rests on familiarity, informal advice or trial and error. This leads to sub-optimal choices that only become apparent after significant implementation effort. Simulator publications make this worse, since they naturally show their own tools under conditions that suit their strengths. What is needed is a common, transparent benchmark of the best simulators on a level playing field, rather than another simulator.
226: The five simulators fall into two families recognized in the literature, and this matters for designing a comparison. Brian2, NEST and Nengo come from computational neuroscience. They integrate differential equations over simulated time and are cited and benchmarked in the neuroinformatics literature ⟦C1:[13]⟧, ⟦C2:[10]⟧, ⟦C3:[14]⟧, ⟦C4:[15]⟧. Their performance reflects that lineage: they prioritize equation-level flexibility and biological fidelity over raw throughput. snnTorch and SpikingJelly come from machine learning. They train by surrogate-gradient backpropagation through time on PyTorch’s tensor runtime, are GPU-accelerated by default, and prioritize training throughput over biological detail. The two traditions rarely appear in the same study, which is part of the gap this thesis addresses.
228: The core problem is that no published study benchmarks Brian2, NEST, Nengo, snnTorch and SpikingJelly together, under identical conditions, on the same hardware. Chapter 2 presents this as three connected parts, each linked below to a research question and objective. First, the benchmark gap: existing studies compare only some of the five, and broad reviews separate biology-oriented simulators from machine-learning-oriented ones rather than testing them together. Second, the measurement problem: direct energy measurement needs specialized neuromorphic hardware. Its standard substitute, the EFLOP metric, is a theoretical estimate never validated against measurements on ordinary processors. So no validated energy proxy exists for the hardware most researchers have. Third, the communication gap: existing results appear as static tables that cannot be filtered by hardware, simulator or experiment type. In short, the problems concern whether the data exist, how reliable some are, and how usable the rest is.
229: The first gap has one property that makes it a research problem rather than a gap in coverage. Every such benchmark reports an ordering. Yet no published SNN benchmark identified in this review reports whether that ordering survives a change in choices its authors did not justify, above all the network size measured and the ranking metric. Neighboring fields already treat this question as part of the method ⟦C1:[16]⟧, ⟦C2:[17]⟧, ⟦C3:[18]⟧ (Section 2.5). SNN benchmarking does not test this stability, and the field’s own benchmark framework ⟦C4:[7]⟧ does not require it. A benchmark that cannot say whether its ranking belongs to the software or the experiment is unfinished. Objective O1 covers both halves: the measurement, and the test of whether its ordering holds.
231: This work uses controlled measurement to establish how the five simulators compare and how far that comparison can be trusted, and releases the suite and dashboard so the evidence can be reproduced. Three research questions, one per gap, guide the work. RQ1: how do the five simulators compare in runtime, memory use, scalability and learning cost under one controlled protocol, and does the ordering hold across the network sizes and metrics a reader might select? It has two halves, because an unstable comparison is not yet a recommendation. It targets measured dimensions rather than a single winner, as each simulator serves a different purpose. RQ2: how valid is a runtime-based energy proxy on commodity hardware relative to the EFLOP metric, by Spearman rank correlation? RQ3: how can a dashboard let a researcher filter and compare results by simulator, backend and experiment type? Three matching objectives answer them. O1: for all five simulators under one protocol on one platform, measure runtime, memory, scalability and learning cost, and quantify by rank correlation how much of the ordering survives a change of size and of metric. O2: build the energy proxy, measure it on commodity hardware, and test it against EFLOP. O3: build and release the dashboard, with a short guide to choosing a simulator.
232: The scope is defined in two ways. First, it covers quantitative performance (runtime, memory, energy and scalability), which matters most to a researcher choosing a simulator under hardware and time constraints. Second, the comparison uses a single hardware platform, so that a runtime difference can be attributed to the simulator rather than the hardware (Section 3.4). Applying the same harness to GPU hardware is a different study and the main item of future work (Section 6.5). The five simulators were chosen for two reasons. Together they broadly cover the main practical uses of spiking networks: biological modeling, large-scale simulation, neuromorphic deployment and machine-learning-style training. All five are also actively maintained with Python interfaces, allowing a controlled, like-for-like implementation.
233: Three delimitations follow, stated so that no reader must infer them. First, the workload is a feedforward leaky integrate-and-fire network with a fixed fan-in of 10 synapses per neuron. No result transfers to recurrent or convolutional spiking architectures without re-measurement. Second, the energy number is a proxy derived from runtime and processor utilization, not a wall-socket measurement. Raffin and Trystram ⟦C1:[19]⟧ show that even hardware-counter-based software energy measurement has domain-dependent error, so the weaker claim made here is the defensible one. Third, the learning experiment reports cost rather than a like-for-like accuracy comparison, because the learning rules tested belong to different classes ⟦C2:[20]⟧ (Section 3.7).
235: The main contribution is a measured result rather than software. For one controlled instrument across eleven execution backends, the ordering of simulators in these five categories is not stable. It depends on the network size measured, and again on the ranking metric. Both shifts are quantified by rank correlation, not asserted (Section 4.10). Four more contributions follow. First, an openly released suite runs identical inference, training and scalability workloads across the five simulators and all eleven executable backends on one machine, keeping every run. Second, a hardware-independent energy proxy, with a validation procedure against an analytic, simulator-independent cost metric and a precise statement of what that validation proves. Third, a dashboard that makes results inspectable as well as readable (Section 3.12). Fourth, a contribution to benchmarking practice: an account of twelve defects in the measurement instruments, five in the harness and seven in the recording and reporting layer. Most had already produced wrong figures before they were found (Section 4.8).
236: The rest of this thesis is structured as follows. Chapter 2 reviews the literature on spiking network foundations, learning paradigms, the available simulators, existing benchmarking studies, benchmark validity and energy measurement, and condenses the analysis into three research gaps. Chapter 3 describes the research design. It covers what a benchmarking dashboard for SNN comparison is and must do, the single-platform scope and its justification, the four experiments, the energy proxy and its validation, and the statistical analysis plan. Chapter 4 reports the results, including a full account of the defects found in the measurement instruments, and answers the research questions. Chapter 5 presents the dashboard as the study's applied artifact, showing its interactive views and what they add beyond the printed figures. Chapter 6 presents the contributions, reflects critically on the work, notes its limitations and proposes extensions to increase its impact.
242: This chapter reviews work relevant to benchmarking SNN simulators. It moves from the fundamentals of spiking computation to the learning paradigms that make training comparisons difficult. It then covers the simulators themselves, existing comparative studies, whether a benchmark's ranking is stable at all, the implementation contexts that give simulator choice practical weight, and energy measurement. The analysis ends in three research gaps, each carried into a research question and objective in Chapter 1 and answered in Chapter 4.
244: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are an energy-efficient alternative to conventional deep neural networks ⟦C1:[1]⟧. Unlike conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs), they rely on discrete spikes and represent time explicitly. A spiking neuron does not propagate continuous activations. It accumulates incoming signals onto a membrane potential and fires only if the potential exceeds a threshold, after which the potential resets. The leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) model captures this with three parameters: a membrane time constant governing decay, a firing threshold and a reset value. It is simple enough to simulate at scale yet keeps the essential temporal dynamics of biological spiking. Because all five simulators studied here support it, it is the natural common denominator for a cross-simulator benchmark.
245: The efficiency argument for SNNs rests on two types of sparsity. The literature broadly agrees on this but disagrees on the size of the savings. Temporal sparsity arises because most neurons are inactive at a given time. Weight sparsity arises because many synaptic weights in trained models are negligible. Narduzzi et al. ⟦C1:[21]⟧ formalized the effect of sparsity with the EFLOP metric, which counts only non-zero operations. They report that SNN inference uses roughly 3.6× fewer effective operations than an equivalent recurrent network below 80% weight sparsity, rising to as much as 8.9× under high sparsity. Ganguly et al. ⟦C2:[22]⟧ supplement this static view.
246: A common concern with using software benchmarks to infer hardware efficiency is whether the two actually correlate. Dey and Dimitrov ⟦C1:[23]⟧ tested this with a sensitivity analysis comparing LIF simulations on Intel Loihi with CPU simulations of the same model. They found close agreement across most parameter configurations. This gives a qualified guarantee that software-level measurements transfer to neuromorphic hardware for standard LIF configurations, an important assumption for any mainly software benchmark such as this one. The guarantee is partial, however: later work on the simulator-to-hardware gap (Section 2.4) shows that transfer depends on the particular tool and device.
247: Finally, the temporal nature of SNN computation calls for a different way of benchmarking training. Newton and Nicola ⟦C1:[24]⟧ compared FORCE-trained spiking networks with rate-based counterparts. Both converged similarly at slow learning rates but diverged at fast ones, where spiking networks learned slowly and had noisy cross-trial firing rates. The methodological consequence is important. Training performance cannot be compared across simulators without controlling for learning rate and rule, because different simulators use different rules and converge at different speeds. Chapter 3 carries this restriction into the benchmark design.
249: The main challenge in training SNNs is that the spike function is not differentiable. Three families of solutions have emerged, and they mirror the design choices of the five simulators. Organizing the literature this way also explains why a fair cross-simulator comparison is hard to design.
250: The first family is unsupervised local learning, typically spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). It adjusts weights by the relative timing of pre- and post-synaptic spikes and is the native rule in Brian2 and NEST. Accuracy has risen steadily. Lee and Sim ⟦C1:[25]⟧ show semi-supervised STDP on standard benchmarks. Yang et al. ⟦C2:[26]⟧ add learned inhibitory weights and Bayesian inference to lift MNIST accuracy above conventional STDP, and Wang et al. ⟦C3:[27]⟧ combine rate and temporal coding for a further ~4.5 per cent gain. Deeper networks are harder, but STDP now reaches deep convolutional networks. Lu and Sengupta ⟦C4:[28]⟧ improve on k-means clustering by 24.56% on Tiny ImageNet with 3.5 times faster convergence. Goupy et al. ⟦C5:[29]⟧ reach 98.56% on MNIST with half the training samples, using voltage-dependent plasticity suited to memristive hardware. The gap with gradient methods is narrowing, but results still involve small datasets. This is itself evidence that STDP-oriented simulators target a different regime from large-scale supervised learning.
251: The second family is surrogate-gradient training. The ill-defined gradient of the spike function is replaced by a smooth approximation in the backward pass, while the forward pass keeps the true spikes. snnTorch uses this approach, which is the easiest entry point for machine-learning researchers. Much recent work reduces the memory and time cost of backpropagation through time. Guo et al. ⟦C1:[30]⟧ combine locally supervised training with temporally truncated BPTT, removing the large memory footprint of the full algorithm. Kim et al. ⟦C2:[31]⟧ share LIF neurons across layers for up to 21.9 times backward-memory efficiency without accuracy loss. Zhang et al. ⟦C3:[32]⟧ use residual learning to reach 94.52 per cent top-1 on CIFAR-10. Yarga and Wood ⟦C4:[33]⟧ cut simulation cost directly, parallelizing the LIF update over time with the ParaLIF neuron for up to 200 times faster training. Recursive least squares is another supervised method. Arthur et al. ⟦C5:[34]⟧ train a million-neuron spiking recurrent network on a GPU roughly 1,000 times faster than an unoptimized CPU reference. This CPU-GPU gap of three orders of magnitude within one method is exactly the hardware-dependent variation a cross-simulator benchmark must quantify rather than assume.
252: The third family is ANN-to-SNN conversion, which transfers the weights of a pre-trained ANN into an SNN and so inherits mature conventional tooling. Progress means closing the accuracy gap and reducing time steps. Li et al. ⟦C1:[35]⟧ reduce conversion error at low latency by initializing the membrane potential and compensating residual rate-coding error. Gao et al. ⟦C2:[36]⟧ embed quantisation-aware training in the conversion, and Yang et al. ⟦C3:[37]⟧ report strong CIFAR-10 and ImageNet results in three time steps. Liu et al. ⟦C4:[38]⟧ distil ANN knowledge layer by layer into SNN Transformers. Liu et al. ⟦C5:[39]⟧ identify an accuracy loss specific to asynchronous hardware and train within that regime. Ororbia ⟦C6:[40]⟧ uniquely proposes a self-supervised contrastive local plasticity rule needing no feedback synapses. Conversion helps when native training is slow or unstable. But it needs a trained ANN, so its cost profile differs from training from scratch.
253: These three families show why benchmarking training across simulators is not like-for-like. Brian2 and NEST use STDP, Nengo uses NEF decoding, and snnTorch trains by surrogate gradients. The simulators therefore solve different optimisation problems and converge at different rates to solutions of different accuracy. Comparing training time per epoch is valid. Comparing final accuracy at a fixed epoch is not, unless the differing learning rules are made explicit. This benchmark therefore reports speed and accuracy together, with appropriate caveats.
254: Two further strands inform the training comparison. The first classifies learning rules by how many signals gate a weight change. Vassallo and Taherinejad ⟦C1:[20]⟧ develop three-factor rules in which a task-carrying signal gates the update, applied to synaptic and axonal delays and weights. They find the rule learns temporal structure that two-factor plasticity cannot. It is the third factor, not the plasticity mechanism, that separates local from gradient learning. This matters because the simulators under test implement rules from different points in that taxonomy, so a fixed sample budget does not treat them equally.
255: The second strand is modern unsupervised spike-timing learning. Dong et al. ⟦C1:[41]⟧ keep the competitive architecture that lets unsupervised STDP separate classes at all, with an adaptive threshold and adaptive lateral inhibition balancing layer activity. They add a temporal-batch update and report the strongest unsupervised-STDP results then published on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. Naderi et al. ⟦C2:[42]⟧ confirm the same requirements using triplet STDP with lateral inhibition and a homeostatic threshold. Both show that the homeostatic machinery is a precondition, not an optimization. Without it, a few neurons potentiate without bound and the labeling step has nothing to separate. In Section 4.8 we report what happens when it is absent, as this literature predicts.
256: A third strand concerns a comparison this thesis cannot make. Lin et al. ⟦C1:[43]⟧ fairly compare learning rules of increasing locality against backpropagation through time and report a trade-off between biological plausibility and performance. Their study compares rules within one implementation; this thesis compares implementations of different rules. The two are complementary. A cross-simulator training comparison ties them together: the cost of a pass depends on the simulator, and the accuracy reached at a fixed budget depends on the rule.
259: The five simulators occupy different positions in a design space set by machine-learning integration and the scale of the target network. Knowing these positions is needed to read any benchmark that places them side by side. The discussion below characterizes each simulator by its design intent, then draws out the consequences for fair comparison.
260: Brian2 is a Python simulator aimed mainly at computational neuroscience. Its core is a domain-specific language that expresses neuron and synapse dynamics in notation close to standard differential equations. Models are therefore readable and easy to modify towards biological detail. Vieth et al. ⟦C1:[44]⟧ compare Brian2 with NEST, ANNarchy and the GPU-accelerated PymoNNtorch. GPU simulation is faster for vectorisable tasks, but Brian2 remains competitive and uniquely flexible for small-to-medium biological models. Its main cost is a first-run compilation of equations to C++, which is slow for small networks but amortized over repeated runs. Linssen et al. ⟦C2:[9]⟧ carried this equation-oriented approach into the NEST ecosystem: their NESTML modeling language generates optimized C++ for NEST and targets SpiNNaker hardware. This shows real convergence between the two neuroscience-oriented tools.
261: NEST works at a very different scale, targeting sparsely connected networks of hundreds of thousands to millions of point neurons. Schmitt et al. ⟦C1:[45]⟧ have shown that NEST scales near-linearly with network size on multi-core CPUs and sustains real-time simulation of a quarter of a million neurons. Section 4.4 measures this strength directly, at sizes two orders of magnitude smaller.
262: Nengo differs from both in its focus on hardware implementation through the Neural Engineering Framework (NEF). The NEF compiles representations of functions into populations of spikes analytically and computes optimal weights instead of learning them. Banerjee et al. ⟦C1:[46]⟧ evaluated NEF-based control of a multi-link pole balancing task on Intel Loihi with seven control and seven neuromorphic metrics. Control quality was comparable to conventional controllers at a fraction of the energy. Uludag et al. ⟦C2:[47]⟧ extended Nengo-style deployment to Izhikevich neurons on Loihi 2. This confirmed that custom neuron models beyond native LIF are feasible on such hardware. Like Brian2, Nengo has a cold-start compilation cost but is efficient during inference. A fair benchmark should therefore report cold-start and warm-state results separately.
263: snnTorch’s close integration with PyTorch has made it the simulator of choice for machine-learning-oriented SNN research. Its surrogate-gradient BPTT training, GPU acceleration and compatibility with the wider PyTorch ecosystem make it the most accessible entry point for deep-learning researchers. Its performance profile is also the most predictable of the four, since it behaves like a standard PyTorch model. Deployment beyond the workstation has also been shown: Jurj ⟦C1:[48]⟧ shows that a network trained off-device and deployed for inference alone runs efficiently on hardware far smaller than the machine that trained it. Xiao et al. ⟦C2:[49]⟧, with their NeuMap toolchain, show that much of the resulting latency and energy depends on how a trained network is mapped onto the hardware, not on the network itself. Thus snnTorch is the simulator with the most predictable efficiency, but with design goals farthest from biological fidelity.
264: SpikingJelly, the fifth simulator, is the one most like snnTorch. Fang et al. ⟦C1:[2]⟧ propose a multi-level design in which the same network definition runs either step by step or fused over the whole simulated window. The fused path uses hand-written CUDA kernels, and they report a training speed-up of approximately eleven times over a step-by-step baseline. Its inclusion here is deliberate. snnTorch and SpikingJelly share a runtime, a training paradigm and a neuron model, so differences measured between them are more credibly due to implementation than to design philosophy. This makes the pair a useful internal control on the whole comparison. Other explanations are possible, since the default kernel selection, tensor layout and data-type handling differ between the two. Section 4.3 reports the measured difference without deciding between them.
265: One caveat applies to how this thesis reads every simulator paper in this section. Each characterizes its own tool under conditions chosen by its authors. The Brian2 code-generation targets are characterized on workloads chosen by the Brian2 team ⟦C1:[8]⟧, ⟦C2:[13]⟧. The cache and spike-delivery design of NEST is evaluated on cortical-scale models by the NEST team ⟦C3:[14]⟧, ⟦C4:[15]⟧. The same holds for the tensor-based libraries ⟦C5:[2]⟧, ⟦C6:[12]⟧. The measurements are not in question; their comparability is. A figure from a different network, size and measurement protocol cannot be set beside another such figure and read as a ranking. Doing so informally is exactly what leaves a practitioner without an evidential basis for choosing.
266: Together, the five simulators show a clear polarity. Brian2 and NEST focus on biological fidelity and accurate neural dynamics, Nengo on deployment to neuromorphic substrates, and snnTorch and SpikingJelly on learning efficiency within a tensor runtime. This polarity is the core of the benchmarking problem: a single experiment favours the design goal it happens to reward and disfavours simulators optimised for a different one. So this thesis runs several experiments, rather than searching for a neutral one that does not exist, and states explicitly which goal each rewards.
267: A 2026 review of the field’s most widely used cross-simulator benchmark shows why this difficult comparison is worth attempting. Even the community's de facto standard benchmark model took years of coordinated effort across simulator teams before results from different codebases could be trusted as truly comparable. The review explicitly calls for more such benchmarks as a guideline for the field ⟦C1:[50]⟧.
268: A wider ecosystem beyond the five target simulators meets specific needs and gives context. Nourse et al. ⟦C1:[51]⟧ validate the SNS-Toolbox for real-time embedded robotic control. Lindqvist and Podobas ⟦C2:[52]⟧ speed up simulation on FPGAs. Gemo et al. ⟦C3:[53]⟧ introduce SHIP for validating novel spiking devices. Panagiotou et al. ⟦C4:[54]⟧ decouple model description from execution. Wang et al. ⟦C5:[55]⟧ present online learning with memory cost linear in network size. Shahsavari et al. ⟦C6:[56]⟧ address distributed communication and synchronization cost. Jurj et al. ⟦C7:[57]⟧ approach usability with a graphical training tool. None is a candidate here, since none is in wide general use. Together, though, they show that efficient spiking simulation is an active field, and that such tools differ on more than speed.
269: Vendor documentation and secondary sources report small-network memory overheads that favour the machine-learning-oriented tools. They cite roughly 120 MB for Brian2, 380 MB for NEST (dominated by MPI initialization), 95 MB for Nengo, and under 50 MB for both snnTorch and SpikingJelly. These are literature claims, not measurements from this study, and Section 4.5 finds the opposite ordering under direct measurement.
272: The closest published comparison is Rudnicka et al. ⟦C1:[58]⟧. They cross three neuron models (leaky integrate-and-fire, metaneurons, probabilistic Levy-Baxter) with three learning rules and report classification performance for each pairing on synthetic spike trains and MNIST. The study is careful within its scope. It sets the premise for this thesis: performance in a spiking system is a property of the combination of model, rule and network size, not of any one alone. But it covers the algorithmic content of a spiking network, not the software that executes it, so it cannot advise on simulator choice. This leaves the cross-category gap addressed here: a researcher weighing a biological simulator against an ML-oriented one has no single, unified comparison to consult.
273: Other studies answer narrower questions, which explains why a performance-first comparison is still missing. Islam et al. ⟦C1:[59]⟧ study ANN-to-SNN conversion for network-on-chip architectures. This matters to hardware designers but is a different question. GenericSNN ⟦C2:[60]⟧ proposes a wrapper API that unifies several simulators, evaluated on functional correctness rather than performance, the opposite priority to this thesis. Gillet et al. ⟦C3:[61]⟧ propose a methodology for evaluating spike-encoding architectures. Xu et al. ⟦C4:[62]⟧ report that simulator-versus-hardware performance can vary from 6 to 300 times depending on the tool-hardware pair. This quantifies the partial software-to-hardware transfer noted in Section 2.1 and makes a systematic multi-simulator comparison more necessary. Community efforts such as Open Neuromorphic benchmark several ML-oriented libraries on GPU training speed and memory, but the results are not peer-reviewed, omit CPU-based and neuroscience simulators, and lack statistical rigor.
274: The picture is consistent. Subsets have been compared, related questions answered, and informal benchmarks exist. Yet no peer-reviewed study evaluates Brian2, NEST, Nengo, snnTorch and SpikingJelly together under identical conditions, with a validated energy proxy, in an accessible interactive form. This is the central gap this thesis addresses, in the data, the energy measurement and the way results are communicated.
275: The closest exception is Kulkarni et al. ⟦C1:[63]⟧. It benchmarks NEST, Brian2, Brian2GeNN, BindsNET and Nengo for speed, flexibility and scalability on single-core, GPU and multi-node hardware, using feed-forward inference, genetic-algorithm and reservoir-computing workloads. Three of its five simulators overlap with this thesis’s set, but the workload and scope do not. It excludes snnTorch and SpikingJelly and does not measure learning cost. It also reports one ordering at one configuration, without testing whether that ordering survives a change of network size or ranking metric. This is a different Kulkarni: the STACS work cited elsewhere in this review ⟦C2:[64]⟧ is a separate 2024 paper by an overlapping author group. It addresses scaling neural simulations, not cross-simulator benchmarking. The lack of a size or metric stability analysis in ⟦C3:[63]⟧ is exactly the structural weakness Section 2.5 develops next.
276: Three recent papers change the standards by which such a study could be judged. NeuroBench ⟦C1:[7]⟧, from a large consortium, is the field’s own attempt at a common vocabulary. Its metrics are meant to travel across implementations: correctness, footprint, connection sparsity, activation sparsity and synaptic operation counts. It targets algorithms and hardware systems, not simulation software, so it does not answer this thesis’s question. It does show that the community itself acknowledges the problem of incomparability. Lin et al. ⟦C2:[43]⟧ give a published head-to-head comparison of learning methods on a level playing field. Cha and Kim ⟦C3:[65]⟧ report the training cost of a direct-training method of the kind any such benchmark must be positioned against. Only ⟦C4:[43]⟧ of the three gives an ordering, and even that does not say whether it would hold if the conditions producing it changed. Neither ⟦C5:[7]⟧ nor ⟦C6:[65]⟧ mentions ranking stability.
277: The comparative literature forms three overlapping traditions. Their conclusions rarely contradict each other because they mostly answer different questions. The first is the single-simulator performance report, in which a simulator’s own authors describe their system. A recent example is the SpikingJelly launch, which showed an eleven-fold training speed-up over a standard baseline ⟦C1:[2]⟧. Such reports are indispensable and often the most technically detailed available. But the comparison is chosen by the party with a stake in the outcome, and the baseline is rarely the strongest competing implementation.
278: The second tradition uses simulators instrumentally, to study architecture or hardware. Work on digital neuromorphic design-space exploration ⟦C1:[62]⟧, runtime construction of large networks ⟦C2:[66]⟧ and full-density cortical models ⟦C3:[50]⟧ reports simulator timings. But the simulator is the apparatus, not the object of study. The results are internally consistent but externally incomparable: the network, time-step, machine and measurement protocol suit the architectural question and are not fixed across studies.
279: The third tradition, to which this thesis belongs, is the deliberate cross-simulator comparison. It is by far the smallest of the three. Vieth et al. ⟦C1:[44]⟧ compare Brian2 with NEST, ANNarchy and a GPU-accelerated PymoNNtorch. They conclude, with qualifications, that Brian2 is competitive for small-to-medium biological models, even if slower on vectorisable workloads. This holds only because the network was fixed across the four systems. Rudnicka et al. ⟦C2:[58]⟧ compare neuron models and learning rules on a common footing, and Islam et al. ⟦C3:[59]⟧ benchmark across the spiking and non-spiking boundary. Golosio et al. ⟦C4:[67]⟧ generalise this comparison to network construction itself. They show a GPU-based approach scaling the construction step of spiking network simulation to up to thousands of GPUs. None of the five simulators studied here targets that regime, which is why the single-machine, single-platform scope of this comparison is stated as a boundary rather than an oversight.
280: Three structural weaknesses recur in the third tradition, and each shapes a design decision here. The first is partial coverage. No published comparison covers both the neuroscience-oriented simulators (Brian2, NEST) and the machine-learning-oriented training libraries (snnTorch, SpikingJelly) within a single harness on a single machine. So measurement has not addressed the most practically consequential question: whether a researcher should reach for a simulator or a training library at all. The second is the missing backend breakdown. Brian2 is typically benchmarked on one code-generation target, most often NumPy, and reported as if that number represented Brian2. Yet Chapter 4 shows that the choice of target changes Brian2's measured runtime by more than an order of magnitude. A single-target number is thus about the target, not the simulator. The third is the missing equivalence check. Comparing runtimes makes sense only if the implementations solve the same problem. In a runtime table, a simulator that is fast because it quietly solves an easier problem looks identical to one that is well engineered.
281: This third weakness deserves emphasis because it is most often left unstated. The tensor-based libraries compute a discrete recurrence over a fixed number of timesteps. The simulators integrate a differential equation with event detection on top. These are not the same calculation, and no amount of care in the timing harness makes them so. What can be done, and is done in Section 3.6 and reported in Chapter 4, is to bound the divergence empirically. Every backend must reproduce the output firing rate of a plain reference implementation within a stated tolerance before its timings are admitted. This does not make the comparison precise. It makes the residual inexactness measurable, which is the most that can honestly be claimed, and more than the comparative literature currently offers.
283: The previous sections summarize what has been measured. This section asks an earlier question. When a benchmark says one system is faster than another, what sort of claim is that, and what would make it hold if asked again? The question is not rhetorical. A benchmark result is the product of a workload, a metric, a machine, a protocol and a set of settings. The experimenter chose most without argument, because something had to be chosen. If the reported ordering changes when one of those choices changes, the ordering describes the choice, not the software.
284: Fields that have faced this question treat it as method. In visual localization, where public leaderboards carry professional stakes, Han et al. ⟦C1:[16]⟧ show how the published ranking of six-degree-of-freedom methods changes when the evaluation protocol is corrected for each dataset’s capture conditions. A ranking is therefore reportable only with that protocol: one that survives a protocol change is a finding; one that does not is an artifact of the evaluation. Shahriari et al. ⟦C2:[17]⟧ make the parallel point for model comparisons: measured performance of an unchanged model shifts across framework versions, so part of what a study reports is a property of the toolchain. Pritchard and Wicenec ⟦C3:[68]⟧ do so for computational workflows, defining formally repeatability, replicability and reproducibility and testing which ones a workflow meets. Ott et al. ⟦C4:[18]⟧ approach it from above, arguing that a leaderboard position is a statement about a benchmark, not a capability.
285: Statistical practice for such comparisons has also moved beyond most benchmark papers. Berrar ⟦C1:[69]⟧ describes how null-hypothesis significance testing is misused when methods are compared across many conditions. Berrar advocates effect sizes and rank-based or Bayesian alternatives alongside or instead of p-values. Gajda and Chlebus ⟦C2:[70]⟧ go further. Ranking models on raw resampled scores, they show, does not establish that a difference between two models is real, since it lacks a significance test and an interpretable scale. Instead they propose a probability-based ranking stating how likely one model is to outrank another. For a simulator benchmark the implication is simple. Runtimes vary by orders of magnitude across network sizes, so a cross-size average is dominated by the largest and unrepresentative of the rest. A rank correlation between orderings at one size and another is scale-free, and answers the question a reader actually has: does the recommendation change?
286: The second threat concerns measurement rather than analysis. Traini et al. ⟦C1:[71]⟧ show that a large fraction of Java microbenchmarks never reach a steady state, and that fixed warm-up budgets bias results systematically, not randomly. A follow-up study by the same group ⟦C2:[72]⟧ replaces the fixed budget with a kernel-based test that decides from the data when a series has reached steady state. This applies to the simulators studied here, which use Python and C++ rather than Java, but pay first-invocation costs of the same kind. Brian2’s standalone target regenerates and compiles C++ on invocation ⟦C3:[8]⟧. The tensor-based libraries pay allocation and kernel-selection costs on their first pass ⟦C4:[2]⟧, ⟦C5:[12]⟧. Nengo solves for decoders before it simulates at all ⟦C6:[10]⟧, ⟦C7:[11]⟧. A protocol keeping warm-up would report the compiler and the allocator. One that silently discards it would hide a real one-off cost to the user. This study therefore times setup separately, discards a stated number of warm-up executions, and reports both. This follows the literature’s first recommendation, but the fixed warm-up count remains a limitation by the steady-state standard of ⟦C8:[72]⟧.
287: The formal discipline for such questions is sensitivity analysis, and its literature bears on Experiment 4, including unflatteringly. Global sensitivity analysis is the standard for models with interacting factors, because varying each factor alone cannot detect an effect that exists only in combination. Puy et al. ⟦C1:[73]⟧ show that, even then, the chosen measure changes which factors are judged important. Newman et al. ⟦C2:[74]⟧ show the same recursion this thesis reports for benchmarks: the importance ranking from a sensitivity analysis itself depends on the chosen workflow. Saxton et al. ⟦C3:[75]⟧ show that conclusions depend on sample size, sampling scheme and total-order estimator. Dey and Dimitrov ⟦C4:[23]⟧ brought the discipline to this domain, separating model behaviour from implementation artefact in point-neuron simulations. Experiment 4 is one-factor-at-a-time, which by the standard of ⟦C5:[73]⟧ is a limitation, not a defense; Section 3.11 states what it can and cannot detect.
288: This gap therefore lies not in the general literature, which has answered the question repeatedly and well, but in this field. It lies within, not alongside, the first of the three gaps this review identifies. No published benchmark of spiking neural network simulators, including the cross-simulator comparisons of Section 2.4, states whether its ordering is robust to a change in network size, metric or its authors’ experimental settings. A benchmark that does not say which of these it relies on has not made a reproducible comparison, however accurate its individual measurements. This is why Section 2.8 describes Gap 1 as the absence of a common benchmark reproducible in this stronger sense, and why Experiment 4 exists.
290: Simulator choice matters most visibly in deployment, where applications have very different performance profiles and no simulator dominates. Adhikari et al. ⟦C1:[76]⟧ propose an energy-aware spiking framework for real-time intrusion detection on power-constrained edge nodes. Chen et al. ⟦C2:[77]⟧ use a multi-level-firing network for satellite orbital-maneuver detection within the size, weight and power constraints of orbital platforms. Pritchard et al. ⟦C3:[78]⟧ propose an end-to-end pipeline for radio-frequency-interference detection on neuromorphic hardware. Partitioning the model across chips matters as much as its size. Chunduri and Perera ⟦C4:[79]⟧ take the other extreme: large-scale sentiment analysis on SpiNNaker, with high accuracy on IMDB at a measured energy cost.
291: Two further studies add robustness and adaptability. Sabatini et al. ⟦C1:[80]⟧ show that recurrent models of orientation selectivity tolerate the device mismatch and analog noise of mixed-signal neuromorphic hardware. This reliability dimension is separate from speed or energy. Max and Shen ⟦C2:[81]⟧ present a neuromorphic olfaction system that learns a new class from a handful of examples and adds classes after deployment. The point is diversity. Different scenarios need different performance dimensions, so a benchmark covering time, memory, energy and scalability lets researchers choose for their setting rather than default to a familiar tool.
292: The deployment literature matters to a benchmark on a commodity processor for an easily overlooked reason. It establishes the commodity processor as a deployment target in its own right, not just a fallback for work that could not reach an accelerator. Inference-only deployment of networks trained off-device ⟦C1:[48]⟧ and mapping of trained networks onto constrained target hardware ⟦C2:[49]⟧ both assume modest executing hardware. Both treat simulator and runtime choice as a decision made once, well before deployment, not one a constrained device can revisit itself.
293: The applied studies make the same point in reverse. Working systems are reported for neuromorphic sentiment analysis ⟦C1:[79]⟧, end-to-end astronomical pipelines ⟦C2:[78]⟧, intrusion detection on constrained edge nodes ⟦C3:[76]⟧ and control applications ⟦C4:[46]⟧. In each case the researcher's practical constraint is the machine on the desk rather than the accelerator in the data center. That reader needs the answer this thesis gives: which simulator is fastest, which scales, and which allocates memory in proportion to the network. The GPU comparison that dominates the benchmarking literature does not answer this.
294: The deployment literature also argues, on methodological grounds, for restricting the comparison to a single platform. Accelerated results are always results about a specific accelerator and software stack. The GPU backends for these simulators are third-party projects with their own release cycles and pinned dependency ranges. Comparing them therefore measures the maturity of four integration efforts at least as much as the simulators. Restricting the comparison to the processor removes that confound. Every simulator here runs its own first-party code path on the same processor, the cleanest available basis for attributing a runtime difference to the simulator. Section 3.4 develops this argument fully.
296: Energy efficiency is the main motivation for SNNs, so how energy is measured is central to any benchmark. The literature offers three classes of method, each with different applicability. The first is direct electrical measurement, such as the on-chip power monitors of Speck ⟦C1:[3]⟧ and Loihi 2 ⟦C2:[4]⟧. It is the most accurate, but it needs specialized hardware and cannot benchmark software on commodity computers. The second is the computational proxy, best exemplified by the EFLOP metric ⟦C3:[21]⟧. Counting non-zero operations at inference time makes it independent of simulator and hardware. For the same reason, it is blind to microarchitectural effects such as cache behavior, memory-bandwidth limits and the cost of moving data between CPU and GPU.
297: The third approach estimates energy from execution time, as the product of runtime, processor utilization and thermal design power. It is the most practical option for software on commodity hardware, but it has not been standardized or validated for cross-simulator comparison. This thesis addresses that gap. The proxy used here is equation (3.8) in Section 3.9, with thermal design power from the vendor datasheet in Table 3.5. Because only processor execution is measured, the accelerator term of a general form is absent. Validity is shown through rank agreement with the EFLOP metric ⟦C1:[21]⟧; absolute accuracy is not claimed. If the proxy ranks simulators in the same order as this theoretical measure, by Spearman correlation, it suits its comparative purpose. It thus sits between the two established classes: more practical than direct measurement, more hardware-aware than a pure operation count, and with an explicit validation criterion.
298: Recent work on software energy measurement sharpens what a runtime proxy can claim, and it counsels caution. Even on-die energy counters have error that depends on the power domain queried, timer granularity and counter overflow ⟦C1:[19]⟧. A software energy figure is thus an estimate with stated uncertainty, not a measurement. Tchakoute et al. ⟦C2:[82]⟧ benchmark CPU and GPU power counters across two tensor frameworks. The figure obtained depends on the framework and the counter queried, so the measurement path is part of the result. Rajput et al. ⟦C3:[83]⟧ show that attributing energy to a code region needs explicit steady-state detection and accounting for measurement overhead. Zschache and Hartwig ⟦C4:[84]⟧ show that the accuracy-energy trade-off varies with deployment configuration, so energy should be reported by condition, not as one headline number. Wang et al. ⟦C5:[85]⟧ make the same point about headline figures: many rest on bottom-up assumptions that cannot be verified against measured consumption.
299: Taken together, this literature does not undermine the use of a proxy. It sets the conditions for using one. A proxy is admissible as an ordinal instrument, comparable within one machine and one session, when the formula, constants and machine are all specified. It is not a quantitative or machine-comparable statement about joules. This thesis adopts that stance, and Section 4.9 reports the evidence for and against the proxy's ordinal validity rather than assuming it.
301: The measurement approaches in the literature divide by what they can observe. This matters because it determines which ones a commodity-hardware study can borrow. Instrumentation is possible only where the silicon exposes it. Studies on Loihi ⟦C1:[4]⟧ and on asynchronous sensing-computing chips ⟦C2:[3]⟧ give truly measured energy figures because the platform provides counters. The satellite resource-management study ⟦C3:[5]⟧ reports similar numbers for the same reason. None of this applies to a general-purpose processor running a Python simulator, where no equivalent per-workload counter is exposed to an unprivileged process.
302: The analytical proxies take the opposite position. They are computed from the workload's structure, not observed from hardware, so they are portable in exactly the way direct methods are not. The most mature example is the EFLOP metric ⟦C1:[21]⟧. It counts the effective operations a spiking workload performs, crediting the sparsity that makes spiking computation attractive. The price of this portability is that an operation count is not an energy measure. The mapping between them depends on the memory hierarchy, the compiler's vectorization and the residency of the working set, and the metric sees none of these.
303: This thesis uses both instruments and presents them side by side, as a methodological choice rather than excess caution. The utilisation-weighted proxy of Section 3.9 is sensitive to what the processor actually did, including thread parallelism a simulator did or did not exploit. But it inherits a configured thermal design power figure, which is a datasheet value, not a measurement. The EFLOP count is blind to the machine but stable. It ignores the execution behaviour that separates a vectorised implementation from a scalar one. The two instruments therefore fail in different directions, and how far they agree on an ordering is itself evidence. Agreement indicates a ranking robust to the choice of instrument. Disagreement localises exactly where an energy claim depends on the measurement method rather than the simulator. Section 4.9 reports the rank correlation specified in Objective O2.
304: Neither instrument makes a claim in joules at the wall plug. Both appear as relative quantities in the dashboard and in Chapter 4, comparable within one machine and one session. The interface makes that scope visible at the point of reading, not in a footnote the reader may not reach.
306: The review converges on three research gaps, each matching one research question and one objective set out in Chapter 1. In turn, they concern data that does not exist, measurements that have not been validated and results that cannot be acted on. One of them includes a requirement the field does not yet meet: a benchmark should determine whether its reported ordering is a property of the software or of the experiment.
307: Gap 1 is the absence of a common, reproducible benchmark across Brian2, NEST, Nengo, snnTorch and SpikingJelly. As Sections 2.3 and 2.4 discussed, existing comparisons cover only subsets or compare the algorithmic content of spiking networks, not the software that runs them ⟦C1:[58]⟧. Others address different questions, such as functional correctness ⟦C2:[60]⟧ or conversion pipelines ⟦C3:[59]⟧. No peer-reviewed study runs all five under the same experiments on the same hardware. Researchers have no objective reference for choosing a simulator.
308: Gap 2 is the lack of a validated, hardware-agnostic energy proxy for commodity hardware. Direct measurement requires special chips ⟦C1:[3]⟧,⟦C2:[4]⟧. The EFLOP metric ⟦C3:[21]⟧ is hardware-agnostic in principle, but it ignores microarchitectural effects and has not been validated against real measurements on ordinary CPUs and GPUs. A runtime-based proxy whose agreement with EFLOP is tested by Spearman rank correlation would give the community a validated reference point for energy claims on standard computers. None currently exists.
309: Gap 3 is the lack of an interactive way to use benchmark data. Where results exist, they appear in static tables that cannot be filtered by hardware, simulator or experiment type, which significantly limits their practical impact. An interactive dashboard letting researchers filter results by their own constraints would turn archived data into actionable guidance.
310: The stability requirement is part of Gap 1, not a separate gap. It is what makes that gap a research problem rather than a coverage gap. Section 2.5 shows that neighboring fields treat stability as part of the method. They report a ranking only with the protocol that produced it ⟦C1:[16]⟧, report the toolchain a measured comparison depends on ⟦C2:[17]⟧, and distinguish repeatability, replicability and reproducibility ⟦C3:[68]⟧. The SNN benchmarking literature, by contrast, reports an ordering and stops. A common benchmark that did the same would close half of Gap 1 (coverage) and leave the other half (reproducibility) open. Objective O1 therefore commits to both: measure the five simulators under one protocol, and quantify how much of the resulting ordering survives a change of size and of metric.
311: These three gaps form one coherent problem. The right data do not yet exist in one place, and where partial data exist, nobody has shown whether their ordering is stable enough to act on (Gap 1). One part of those data, the energy figure, cannot yet be trusted without validation (Gap 2). And even where the data exist, they cannot support a decision (Gap 3). Solving any one gap alone leaves the problem unsolved. Measurements without a stability test give an ordering of unknown durability. An interface without measurements has nothing to show. A stability test without an interface cannot reach the reader who needs it.
316: This chapter describes how the study was conducted, in enough operational detail for another researcher to repeat it and obtain comparable numbers. One design feature is stated at the outset rather than left to inference: the comparison runs on a single hardware platform (Section 3.4). Section 6.5 describes extending the same harness to GPU hardware as the main item of future work.
317: Weaknesses in the design were found after the first round of measurement, and two components were added. Experiment 4 is a sensitivity analysis that tests whether the simulator ordering withstands the experimenter's arbitrary choices. The energy proxy also gained a validation procedure against a hardware-agnostic theoretical cost metric, which the original design described but did not operationalize. Both are presented as part of the method, not as extensions, because a benchmark that reports an ordering without testing its stability is incomplete.
319: The title of this thesis is the name of an artifact, not a question. Before describing the design behind it, the phrase is worth unpacking. A benchmarking dashboard for SNN comparison combines three things. The first is a fixed workload, executed identically. The second is an instrument that measures what that workload costs in each spiking neural network simulator. The third is an interface that lets a reader interrogate the measurements instead of receiving a conclusion. Each carries a requirement, and the rest of this chapter operationalizes them.
320: The comparison in this study is between simulators, not models. The scientific object is the software. The same leaky integrate-and-fire network, with the same number of neurons, connectivity, integration timestep and input statistics, is expressed once for each simulator and then run. Nothing else was allowed to vary, so any difference in runtime, memory or spike count that survives this construction is a difference between implementations. For this reason, the unit of comparison is the simulator-backend pair, not just the simulator. Brian2 running through its C++ standalone target and Brian2 running through its NumPy target are the same library but not the same instrument. A figure reporting just “Brian2” would report whichever of the two happened to be selected.
321: Benchmarking is what makes the comparison a measurement rather than a demonstration. A benchmark is defined by its protocol, not its result. The protocol states the workload, the number of discarded warmup executions, the number of retained executions, the statistic computed over them and the environment in which it all ran. If any of these is left implicit, a difference between two published figures cannot be attributed: it could be the software, the protocol or the machine. Sections 3.6 to 3.9 give the full protocol. The environment is recorded programmatically at run time, not transcribed by hand, so the record cannot drift from the run that produced it.
322: The third component is the dashboard, which is often treated as decoration but is not treated that way here. Results in this field are traditionally published as a table of medians. Such a table hides exactly what a reader needs to act on: how much individual runs varied, whether the ordering holds at the network size the reader intends to run, whether an entry is a measurement or a placeholder, and how far the figure would move under a different but equally defensible metric. In this thesis, a dashboard is an interface over the stored measurements that makes these four properties directly inspectable. Section 3.12 gives the controls that do this.
323: This definition implies three properties worth stating, because they set this artifact apart from a results page. The dashboard only reads; it never writes. First, it has no measurement logic of its own, so it cannot display a quantity the harness did not measure. Second, one implementation of one query generates each figure, table and exported file (Section 3.12). Third, the dashboard reports the conditions under which its own rankings fail, instead of presenting a single ordering as unconditional. The sensitivity analysis of Section 3.11 provides exactly that information, and the interface shows it beside the rankings it qualifies.
324: It is equally useful to say what the artifact is not. It is not a leaderboard. No simulator is declared the winner, because the measurements in Chapter 4 show that the ordering changes with network size and with the chosen metric, so a single ranking would misrepresent the data it came from. It is not a profiler. It does not run the simulators, and it charges cost to a condition rather than a line of code. Nor is it a recommendation engine. It is a selection guide, telling the reader which measured property matters for which intended use. The choice stays with the reader, since only they know the network size and intended learning mechanism. In this sense the dashboard is itself a research instrument, whose design choices are as much part of the contribution as the numbers it displays. It fulfills Objective O3.
328: One workload expressed once per simulator, one measurement protocol writing to an append-only database, and one interface for interrogating the stored measurements.
330: The study is a quantitative, controlled computational experiment. The independent variable is the simulator, or more precisely the simulator-backend pair. Two of the five simulators expose more than one execution backend, and those backends differ from each other more than the simulators do. The dependent variables are wall-clock runtime, peak process memory, processor utilization, an energy proxy derived from the first and third of these, classification accuracy where a simulator is trained, and the fitted exponent describing how runtime grows with network size.
331: We impose control by giving each simulator the same network specification, integration timestep, input statistics and measurement protocol. We also take every comparison from one measurement session on one machine, so no comparison crosses a hardware or software change. The constraint applies at both measurement and analysis. Every query behind every figure in Chapter 4 is limited to the machine that produced the campaign. Section 4.8 records what happened on the one occasion that restriction was absent. What cannot be controlled is that each simulator implements the specification with its own solver and data structures. This is not a confound to remove; it is the very thing being measured.
332: The experimental design is a full factorial over simulator-backend pair and network size for Experiments 1 and 3, and a single-factor comparison for Experiment 2. Experiment 4 is different in kind. It makes no new measurements. It recomputes the ordering the other three produce under each measured network size and each recorded metric, and asks how far those orderings agree. Since we compare within a single dataset, not across different runs, the other possible explanations for a change in order (different hardware, a different network definition, a different protocol) are fixed by construction. Only the choice of size and metric remains.
336: Each research gap has one research question, answered by one stated experiment and one stated analysis, which discharges one objective.
337: Figure 3.3 shows the instrument that carries the design. Its central property is that the measurement code is written once and shared by all backends, so no simulator gets an instrument of its own.
340: (One model specification maps to one adapter per execution backend. A single instrumented runner measures each backend identically and writes one row per individual run.)
342: All measurements in this thesis were performed on a single processor-based platform, kept constant for the entire campaign. The rest of the design depends on this controlled-experiment choice. The benchmark can assign a difference in cost to a difference in software. But any variation in the machine (a different processor, memory subsystem or thermal envelope) enters the measurement as a second explanation for every observed difference. No later analysis can separate it from the first. Fixing the machine removes the second explanation by construction.
343: This choice means we cannot quote an absolute timing as a property of a simulator: the milliseconds in Chapter 4 are specific to this platform. In return, every ordering, fitted scaling exponent and rank correlation reported there is a statement about simulators, not machines. These are the results this study offers. Section 3.14 records the platform programmatically at run time, not by transcription, so the environment behind any figure can be checked rather than assumed. Appendix B gives its full capability profile.
344: The study is scoped to processor-based simulation, which is where the choice between these simulators is actually made. A researcher picks a simulator, writes a model and runs it on the machine in front of them long before any accelerator or neuromorphic device is involved. The deployment literature reviewed in Section 2.6 supports treating that setting as a target in its own right, not a fallback. Applying the same harness to accelerator hardware is a separate study with its own design requirements, set out in Section 6.5 as the principal item of future work.
350: (Every quantity except the executing simulator is held identical across simulators and backends, so a difference in measured cost can be attributed to the software.)
352: The first experiment measures the cost of the simplest meaningful spiking computation: one forward pass of a feedforward network of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons, without learning. It aims to isolate each simulator's native execution overhead from the variation learning introduces. Each simulator builds the network in Table 3.2, receives Poisson input at the same rate and is timed over the same simulated interval.
