374: The second experiment concerns learning, and its purpose must be stated exactly, since a loose statement would promise a comparison the design cannot deliver. Experiment 2 measures and reports the cost of learning: what one pass of each simulator's native update rule costs in wall-clock time, memory and processor utilization, on the same network topology and task. It is a fixed-budget result, not a converged one, and not a measure of simulator quality. Each simulator is trained with its native learning mechanism, because imposing an alien rule measures the researcher's implementation of that rule, not the tool. snnTorch and SpikingJelly train by surrogate-gradient backpropagation through time ⟦C1:[12]⟧, ⟦C2:[86]⟧. Nengo solves Neural Engineering Framework decoders in closed form ⟦C3:[10]⟧. Brian2 and NEST use unsupervised spike-timing-dependent plasticity followed by a neuron-labelling pass, in the architecture current work in that line retains: an adaptive firing threshold, lateral inhibition and weight normalization ⟦C4:[41]⟧, ⟦C5:[42]⟧. As executed, the training path timed this cost in wall-clock time only. Memory and processor utilization were not observed during training, a limitation reported in Section 4.6.
375: One network parameter needs explicit statement, because every training figure in Chapter 4 depends on it. The architecture has three layers throughout: 784 input units, a hidden layer of 256 leaky integrate-and-fire neurons, and ten output units, one per class. The confirmation report proposed a hidden layer of 500. The narrower layer is used here for two reasons. First, it keeps the training budget as the only difference between the fixed-budget results in Section 4.6 and the full reference configuration. A change in accuracy between them then has one candidate explanation, not two; the same argument fixes the budget across simulators below. Second, it keeps every training figure in this thesis at a single width, which a chapter mixing two widths could not claim. The report's hardware plan was superseded in the same way and for the same reason: what is reported here is the configuration actually measured.
376: The consequence is stated openly, and it is why the experiment is built around cost. Comparing training time per epoch across simulators is legitimate, because it gives the price of one pass of each simulator's native update on an identical network. Comparing final accuracies does not compare simulator quality on equal terms. The simulators solve different optimization problems, and their sample efficiency differs by orders of magnitude. The three-factor rules studied in ⟦C1:[20]⟧ gate plasticity with a task signal that local two-factor rules lack. Rules from these classes are therefore not interchangeable at a single shared budget. Recent work mindful of this distinction reports accuracy against a stated budget rather than as a converged figure ⟦C2:[87]⟧, and this study does the same.
377: Two more design decisions follow. First, every simulator and backend that supports training gets the same budget, not one scaled to its capacity: 6,000 training and 1,000 test images over three epochs. Nengo's closed-form solve has no epoch to repeat, so it is measured once over the same 6,000 images. Fixing the budget removes it as a confounding explanation for accuracy differences. What remains is due to the learning rule and its cost per image, and the budget appears beside every accuracy number so none is read without it. Second, the cost of the full reference configuration (60,000 training and 10,000 test images over ten epochs) was first projected from measured per-image cost, not executed, and Table 4.5 presented it as a projection. It has since been run in full for all nine backends, and Table 4.5 now reports the measured cost beside the projection. Projection was the right choice at design time. At the measured per-image cost, a full run would have taken roughly three and a half to forty-five hours for the plasticity-based rules, depending on backend. The gradient-based libraries would have needed under half an hour, and Nengo's single solve seconds. Running them all then would have used the machine time the scalability sweep needed. When run afterwards, the full configuration took 3.5 to 38.4 hours for the plasticity-based rules, 14.9 to 15.4 minutes for the gradient-based libraries and 3.54 seconds for Nengo's solve. The projection sits beside the per-image cost so readers can recompute it for their own budget or machine.
378: Before this experiment, two corrections were applied to the learning implementations, and a third defect was found, left uncorrected and reported as a finding. Section 4.8 documents all three. The first bug was in the NEST adapter, whose spike-counting routine scaled quadratically with the number of images presented. The second was the weight-freezing mechanism for the labeling and evaluation passes: it queried the wrong population and did nothing, so accuracy was measured on a network still learning. Third, none of the spike-timing-dependent-plasticity adapters implemented the full homeostatic machinery the method relies on ⟦C1:[41]⟧, ⟦C2:[42]⟧. This omission is reported, not repaired. It makes accuracy fall as the training set grows, which is the behavior the literature predicts without that machinery, and reporting it is more informative than quietly removing it.
379: The warm-up protocol (Section 3.6) follows the performance-engineering literature on warm-up bias and steady-state detection discussed in Section 2.5 ⟦C1:[71]⟧, ⟦C2:[72]⟧. Pritchard and Wicenec ⟦C3:[68]⟧ give the vocabulary for what this supports: the study repeats and replicates within one platform but does not claim reproduction across platforms.
381: The third experiment replicates the inference workload across five network sizes spanning two orders of magnitude and fits a power law to the results. Speed at a single operating point cannot show whether a simulator is fast because of low fixed overhead or because of low per-neuron cost. These two properties call for different decisions as a model grows. The fitted exponent k is the slope of log(runtime) vs. log(N). A value of k ~ 1 means cost scales with network size; k ~ 0 means fixed overhead dominates runtime.
382: The coefficient of determination and the standard error of the slope are reported with the exponent, which alone would be incomplete. A power law fitted to five points can look convincing yet describe the data poorly, and a reader cannot tell the difference from the exponent alone.
383: Five sizes are used: 100, 500, 1 000, 5 000 and 10 000 neurons, spanning two orders of magnitude. The lower bound is chosen so that fixed per-run overhead stays visible rather than amortized away. A simulator whose cost at 100 neurons is dominated by setup shows a property a practitioner needs to know about. A sweep starting at a size large enough to hide it would hide the finding rather than measure it. The upper bound is set so that every simulator can run the complete protocol on the reference machine in one session, and no backend has a shorter sweep than another.
384: The exponent comes from ordinary least-squares regression of the base-ten logarithm of median runtime on the base-ten logarithm of network size. This gives the slope k in the power law, with runtime proportional to N to the power k. Three quantities are kept with the slope: its standard error, the 95 per cent confidence interval derived from it (Student t distribution, three degrees of freedom), and the coefficient of determination. The last is not ornamental. A fitted exponent describes the data only if a straight line in log-log space does, yet a backend whose runtime has no systematic relation to network size still yields a regression slope. Reporting that slope without its coefficient of determination would pass off a number with no referent as a genuine scaling result. Below a coefficient of 0.25, the analysis and dashboard omit the exponent and report the series as flat.
385: This precaution is not hypothetical. The backend yields an exponent indistinguishable from zero: its runtime does not respond to a hundredfold change in network size, which no simulator's workload does (Section 4.7). The cause is that the fitted quantity is compilation time, not simulation time. Comparing the fitted exponent with the absolute runtime at each size reveals this, which is why both are reported together throughout.
387: This study's instrumentation cannot measure energy directly, so a proxy is used: runtime multiplied by utilisation-scaled thermal design power, integrated over the measured interval. The formula assumes that power draw is roughly linear with utilisation, and that the manufacturer's thermal design power figure holds for the processor and chassis used.
389: where U is average processor utilization over the measured interval, as a percentage. The two numerator terms are the user-mode and system-mode processor time used in that interval by every thread of the process and by the child processes it waited for. They are read from the kernel's per-process CPU clock, not sampled. ΔT is the wall-clock duration of the same interval. Values above 100 per cent indicate real multi-core execution. An earlier, sampled form of this measurement was defective; Section 4.8 documents it.
391: where E is the energy proxy in joules, T the measured runtime in seconds, and the last term the platform's thermal design power in watts, as stated and sourced in Table 3.5.
393: This is what equation (3.8) reduces to once (3.7) is substituted. The proxy is processor-seconds valued at thermal design power, which is why it is validated by its ordering and not by its joule values.
394: Neither assumption can be verified without a power meter. The study instead tests the weaker but still useful question RQ2 asks: does the proxy order computations the same way as a hardware-independent theoretical measure of the work? That reference is the synaptic operation count, calculated analytically from the network specification as expected presynaptic spikes times fan-out. It depends only on the workload, and it is identical across simulators at a given size because every simulator builds the same network.
396: where the synaptic term counts one accumulate per spike delivered across a fan-in of F synapses, and Φ is the effective operation count. The membrane term counts one multiply-accumulate per neuron per step for the membrane leak. Φ depends only on the network specification. It is therefore constant across simulators at a given size and can act as the independent reference for the proxy.
398: the expected number of spikes from N Poisson sources at rate r over the simulated interval, used in equation (3.10) where an adapter reports only its output spike count.
399: The validation has three steps. First, the Spearman rank correlation between the proxy and the synaptic operation count across the size sweep, per backend, tests whether the proxy tracks the work. Second, regressing log energy on log runtime shows how much of the proxy is just rescaled time. If utilisation barely varies, the proxy adds nothing runtime does not already carry. Third, a sensitivity analysis re-derives the ordering with thermal design power varied ±30% and the utilisation exponent between 0.8 and 1.2, and measures rank agreement with Kendall's tau. The proxy can still select a simulator when its absolute joules cannot, provided the ordering survives errors in its own parameters.
401: Interpretation is defined a priori and the reasoning for each choice is explained, so a reader can openly disagree with it instead of having to reverse-engineer it.
405: Coefficient of variation: for a condition with retained runtimes r₁,..., r₅, median m and sample standard deviation s (n − 1 = 4 in its denominator), equation (3.12) gives it as a percentage. Dividing by the median rather than the mean keeps it robust to the occasional slow run of a right-skewed runtime distribution.
407: Shapiro-Wilk normality test: the statistic W for a condition's five retained runtimes measures how closely their order statistics match those expected under normality; W near one means a good match. With only five observations the test has little power against non-normality. It is therefore reported per backend (the statistic and whether it rejects normality at 0.05), not used to justify a blanket assumption either way.
409: Welch's one-way ANOVA and effect size: Welch's F-test compares k group means without assuming equal variances, using the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation for its denominator degrees of freedom. Eta-squared, from the same sums of squares as the classical ANOVA, gives the share of variance due to backend rather than noise. In Section 4.3, F(10, 17.22) = 1898.78 across k = 11 backends gives eta-squared = 0.9986. Essentially all variance in the pooled sample comes from backend, not run-to-run noise.
410: Pairwise Welch's t-test with Holm correction and Cohen's d: each pair of backends is compared with Welch's t-test (no equal-variance assumption). P-values are corrected for the number of comparisons with the Holm step-down procedure, at least as powerful as a flat Bonferroni correction. Cohen's d accompanies each p-value because, with five observations per side, the corrected p-value alone underestimates separation. Eleven backends give C(11,2) = 55 pairs, and Section 4.3 reports which separate at 0.05 after correction. A comparison involving a group that already failed Shapiro-Wilk is flagged, not silently trusted.
412: Welch's statistic, which does not assume equal variance between the two groups. For group i, x̄i, si and ni are the mean, sample standard deviation and size.
414: Cohen's d uses the pooled standard deviation. Reporting it pairs an unequal-variance test (Welch's t-test, equation 3.13) with an effect size based on the pooled standard deviation (equation 3.14), which assumes equal variances. The asymmetry is accepted because Cohen's d is a descriptive supplement to the corrected p-value, not the basis for the significance decision. It therefore does not affect which pairs are called separated.
417: Fitted by ordinary least squares, so that T ∝ Nᵏ.
422: where dᵢ is the difference between the two ranks assigned to item i and n is the number of items. It applies when the relationship under test is assumed monotonic but not necessarily linear.
423: Energy proxy: equation (3.8), with thermal design power stated and sourced in Table 3.5. It estimates energy rather than measuring it, so Section 3.9 validates its ordering against a hardware-independent measure instead of trusting its absolute joule values.
424: Two limits are stated here rather than in the results. First, repeats within a condition are not strictly independent: they run consecutively in one process on one machine, sharing cache state and thermal history. The measured range thus reflects run-to-run variability within a session, not the full variability of the measurement. Second, five observations per group is a small sample. At this size Shapiro-Wilk has little power to detect non-normality, so a group that passes is not proven normal, only not shown otherwise. One of the eleven backends fails it outright. Section 4.3's pairwise comparisons carry that caveat, with Cohen's d beside every p-value as a check that does not depend on normality.
426: The main finding of this thesis is an ordering. It is worth reporting only if it belongs to the simulators, not to the settings used to compare them. Every benchmark in this field automatically fixes two such settings: the network size at which results are reported, and the quantity used for ranking. Experiment 4 varies each in turn and asks whether the ordering survives, discharging the second half of Objective O1 and RQ1. Its instrument is the one adjacent fields use for exactly this purpose: recompute the ranking under a changed condition and report the agreement between the orderings as a rank correlation. This follows the practice Han et al. ⟦C1:[16]⟧ argue for in benchmark evaluation.
427: One design boundary is declared here, not left to the results: Experiment 4 varies one condition at a time. Puy et al. ⟦C1:[73]⟧ treat global sensitivity analysis, which varies factors jointly, as the standard for interacting effects, since a one-factor-at-a-time design cannot detect an effect that exists only in combination. The design here answers a bounded, practical question instead: can either choice alone overturn the ordering? Section 6.5 sets out what the joint question would take. Two more caveats from this literature carry into the reporting. The ranking a sensitivity analysis produces depends on the chosen workflow ⟦C2:[74]⟧, and its findings depend on sample size and estimator ⟦C3:[75]⟧. Section 4.10 therefore reports the number of backends and orderings behind each coefficient, not just the coefficient.
430: Experiment 4 needs no new measurement: both comparisons are recomputed from the Experiment 3 scalability sweep. This counts in favour of the method and is not a shortcut. The test costs a benchmark one more analysis of data it already holds, which is the whole argument for making it routine. The outcome measure is rank agreement: Kendall's tau-b between the orderings under the changed and reference conditions. A coefficient near one means the condition changes magnitudes but not which simulator a researcher should adopt. A coefficient near zero marks a choice the recommendation is conditional on.
434: (The rank correlation between two orderings of the same backends, compared pair by pair, measures whether the ranking is a property of the simulators or of the experimental settings.)
436: The study's applied artifact is the dashboard, a browser application over the results database that lets a researcher filter by simulator, backend and experiment. Its design requirement, derived from RQ3, is that someone choosing a simulator can reach the number relevant to their situation without reading the thesis.
437: The navigation reflects this directly. Each experiment has its own address rather than a tab inside one document, behind a persistent sidebar that marks the current page: Dashboard, Inference, Scalability, Memory, Training, Sensitivity and Equivalence & Provenance. A reader can therefore bookmark, reload or share the page relevant to their question, and the browser back button works as it does elsewhere on the web.

Brian2's three code-generation targets differ by more than two orders of magnitude on the same processor, so a row labelled only “Brian2, CPU” would give one backend's figure to the whole simulator. The interface therefore exposes backend, which every stored row records. There is no hardware control: every row was measured on one platform, and a control implying otherwise would misrepresent the data.
439: Each row also has a provenance flag, shown in the interface, marking it as a measurement or a placeholder. In research, a dashboard that cannot tell a measured number from one seeded for layout is a liability, however convenient the placeholders were during development.
440: The dashboard fulfils Objective O3 under two rules. They are stated here because both are visible in the interface and always applied.
441: First, nothing is shown without a value. A dash, zero or empty cell for an unmeasured quantity looks like a genuine zero, so every gap is named in words instead of left as a blank chart position. A simulator that would not install says so, as does a backend with no rows for a task. Second, nothing that changes the dataset is exposed. An earlier version had a control that cleared measured rows before an abbreviated re-run, and it once destroyed a complete result set. Starting a campaign is deliberately left to the command-line harness. The dashboard only reads, and its export serialises the rows on screen without writing anything back.
442: The dashboard has one shared data layer and two presentation layers. The data layer is a single Python module with no web-framework dependency. It runs every database query, the scaling regression, the equivalence-log parsing and every ranking. It can be exercised directly from an interpreter, which is how the Chapter 4 figures were checked against the interface. On top sit a server-rendered Flask implementation with client-side charting and a pure-Python Streamlit implementation, verified to return identical values for every derived quantity. They serve different readers: one needs only a lightweight dependency, the other no hand-written JavaScript. A figure in this thesis, a figure in either interface and a row in an exported file all come from one implementation of one query, so they cannot disagree. The browser front end draws every chart with a small local module, not a third-party content-delivery network, so it renders without an internet connection and can be audited in full.
443: Three presentation decisions follow from the data, not taste. Colour: eleven execution backends need more hues than a reader can reliably distinguish, so colour marks the simulator and line style marks the backend within it. The six colours were tested for separation under normal and simulated colour-vision-deficient vision, and for contrast against the background. Hue answers which simulator; stroke answers which backend. Colour follows the entity, not its rank, so removing a backend from a chart never repaints the rest.

The plain reference implementation is a control. It shows what the same network costs with no simulator at all, and letting it win would answer a question nobody asked. Compiler-dominated backends report a compiler's time, not a simulator's, so they are not comparable on runtime, scaling or memory. Both exclusions are shown directly below the affected figures and labelled in the detailed tables, so a reader sees what was left out and why.
445: Dispersion: a median from five tightly clustered runs and one from five scattered runs are different claims, yet a bar chart treats them alike. Because the harness stores every run, not just the aggregate, the dashboard shows the underlying distribution by default. Every median in the detailed tables comes with its coefficient of variation.
446: The sidebar leads to six experiment views: inference cost, scalability, memory, supervised training, sensitivity, and equivalence together with the machine, package and parameter provenance captured programmatically at run time. This lets a reader establish what was measured, and on what, before interpreting a figure. A seventh page lists the research gaps addressed, each mapped to a research question and objective. It gives a qualitative simulator-selection guide and states plainly what the measurements do not establish. This page turns a table of numbers into advice a reader can act on, and it most directly serves the practical purpose Chapter 1 sets for the comparison.
447: Filtering is by backend and works identically in every view. Controls can hide the control implementation and compile-dominated backends for readers who want only directly comparable rows. Filtering happens only in the presentation layer and never issues a different query, so no interaction can change which measurement is under discussion. Every view exports the rows behind its figures through the same code path, so an export cannot drift from its chart.
448: Figure 3.7 shows the dashboard architecture. Its defining property is that no query is written twice.
451: (Both front ends share configuration, presentation and data access, so one implementation of one query produces a figure, a table and an exported file.)
453: Reliability rests on repetition and seeding. Every random process is seeded identically across simulators. Each condition follows the warm-up and retention protocol of Section 3.6, and every comparison is drawn from one measurement session on one machine (Section 4.2). Run-to-run dispersion is reported as a coefficient of variation and a full measured range, so readers can judge stability directly rather than infer it from the median.
454: Internal validity rests on the implementations being equivalent. Before timing begins, each simulator's network is checked for firing rates within tolerance of the others. This check is necessary but not sufficient, a residual risk Section 4.12 discusses.

The workload is a feedforward network of fixed fan-in, so nothing here should be extrapolated to recurrent or convolutional spiking architectures.
456: Reproducibility is addressed by releasing the harness, the exact commands, the results database with per-row provenance, and the analysis pipeline that produces every figure and table in Chapter 4. Every figure in this thesis is computer-drawn, and the browser interface renders with no internet access (Section 3.12). This matters for a marking session, an air-gapped lab or a laptop on a train.
460: Table 3.5 gives the environment. It was captured programmatically at run time, not transcribed by hand, because an earlier draft reported a combination of library versions that cannot coexist, and the incompatibility went unnoticed until traced. The machine is the researcher's own laptop. It runs the suite inside WSL2, with thirty-two logical cores available to the process. This cuts the other way from a constrained instance: the thread-parallel configurations have real room to show an advantage, so a configuration that still shows none is reporting a property of its own design rather than a hardware ceiling.
462: The study involves no human or animal participants and no personal data. MNIST is a standard public dataset, freely available for research. The ethical obligations that do apply are those of computational research reporting. Measurements are reported as measured. Absent results are shown as absent, not omitted. Defects found in the researcher's own instruments are disclosed with their corrections. The artifacts are released so the claims can be verified. Section 4.8 deals with the third of these. It sits in the results chapter rather than an appendix, because the state of the instruments is part of the result.
464: The study is a controlled experiment on one hardware platform, with five simulators and eleven executable backends; accelerator execution is left as future work. Three experiments measure inference cost, learning cost and scaling behavior. A fourth recomputes the resulting ordering under every network size and every measured metric, and reports how far those orderings agree. The energy proxy is validated against a simulator-independent theoretical cost metric. The statistical plan tests its own parametric assumptions instead of assuming them, and reports effect sizes throughout. The limits of what it can establish at this sample size are stated in advance, not discovered in the results. Chapter 4 reports what this design produced.
469: This chapter describes what the Chapter 3 design produced and compares it with the literature in Chapter 2. Four experiments are presented: inference cost at a fixed network size, learning cost and accuracy,

A capability finding records whether a configuration could run at all and, if not, why not. An interpretation links these to the literature. 506: The exponents divide the configurations into two regimes. Nengo is steepest at k = +1.550, more than proportional to network size. NEST follows at k = +1.199, +1.195 and +1.151 with one, four and two threads, and the scalar NumPy control is almost exactly proportional at k = +0.993. At the other end, Brian2's three targets sit at k = +0.048, +0.023 and +0.001. A configuration whose runtime does not scale with the problem is not measuring the problem, and Section 4.7 explains what these three measure instead.
507: Four fits need caution, and the figure shows them that way rather than as bare point estimates. Brian2/C++ standalone (R² = 0.013), Brian2/Cython (0.330), Brian2/NumPy (0.688) and snnTorch/CPU (0.866) all follow a single power law only loosely. For the Brian2 targets this is the finding itself, not a defect in the fit: a poor power-law fit is what a runtime independent of network size looks like. For snnTorch the exponent is better read as a summary of the trend, and the measured points in Table 4.3 are the more trustworthy statement.
508: The speed ordering is not stable across the sweep; the clearest evidence is the individual movements, not a summary statistic. Nengo starts mid-pack and drops from rank 5 to rank 11 (last of eleven) between the smallest and largest measured network. Brian2/NumPy climbs from rank 9 to rank 2, and Brian2/Cython from rank 10 to rank 3. NEST/4-threads drops from rank 2 to rank 5, NEST/2-threads from rank 3 to rank 4, and NEST/1-thread from rank 4 to rank 6. Counting only simulator configurations, the four fastest at one hundred neurons are NEST/4-threads, NEST/2-threads, NEST/1-thread and Nengo. At ten thousand they are Brian2/NumPy, Brian2/Cython, NEST/2-threads and NEST/4-threads. The fastest at the small end is not the fastest at the large end. Nengo, the fourth-fastest simulator configuration at a hundred neurons, ends up last of all eleven backends at ten thousand.
509: Across all eleven backends, Kendall's tau-b between the orderings at one hundred and at ten thousand neurons is 0.273. A tau of one would mean identical orderings; at 0.273, only 35 of the 55 pairs are ordered the same way and 20 the opposite way. Section 4.10 gives the coefficients at the other sizes, where they are the main result, and explains why no p-value is given.
510: A single session cannot show whether these movements exceed the noise of measuring the same thing twice. The sweep was therefore compared across the four sessions that measured it on this laptop: the session reported here, its twin run ten minutes later with the same instrument, the August campaign and the September full-scale campaign. All four timed runtimes with the same high-resolution clock. At any fixed size, the ordering from another session agrees with this session's at tau = 0.745 to 1.000 (the twin: 0.891 or better). Within any one session, the ordering at one hundred neurons agrees with the ordering at ten thousand at only tau = 0.200 to 0.273. The weakest point of the sweep lies between 0.127 and 0.273 in every session, although where it falls is not reproducible (five hundred neurons here, one thousand in August). Network size moves the ordering far more than re-measuring does. Absolute times reproduce less well. Over a ten-minute interval, every condition of the size sweep in the twin session lies within -21% to +15% of this one. Between days, however, the multi-threaded configurations move much further. NEST at ten thousand neurons ran 1.4 to 2.8 times slower in this session than in the two earlier campaigns, and Nengo at one thousand neurons ran 7.1 times slower than in August. The cause of that between-day variation was not measured and is not asserted here. It is the ordering and the exponents that reproduce, not the times, and this chapter's claims are made at that level.
513: (A line crossing another marks a pair of configurations whose relative standing depends on the size at which the benchmark was run. A benchmark that reports one operating point cannot see this effect or warn about it.)
514: This is the strongest argument for this thesis's multi-size design. A study reporting a single operating point would have given a defensible-looking answer to RQ1. It would have had no way of knowing that the answer flips within the range of sizes a researcher would plausibly use.
515: The result also refines, rather than contradicts, a finding in the literature. Schmitt et al. show that NEST scales near-linearly with network size on multi-core CPUs and present this linearity as a strength, demonstrated in real time with a quarter of a million neurons. Here NEST's exponents are 1.151 to 1.199, close to proportional but slightly steeper, at sizes two orders of magnitude smaller. At these sizes the same property is a liability rather than an asset. The two results do not conflict: whether near-linear scaling is desirable depends entirely on the operating regime, and the current simulator-selection literature does not make that distinction.
519: (The figure includes the interpreter and every imported library. This is why the lines start high, and why Section 4.5 reads growth across the sweep rather than the value at any single size.)
520: At the largest measured network, peak resident set size is 641.7 MB for Brian2's NumPy target and 2,203.8 MB for Nengo's reference simulator (a factor of 3.4). At the reference size, the eleven backends do not cluster together but split into two distinct groups. NEST sits between 91 and 94 MB for its three thread counts. All the other backends (the two NumPy reference implementations, Nengo, SpikingJelly, snnTorch and all three Brian2 targets) sit between 629 and 694 MB. This difference is almost entirely a matter of which process is measured. NEST is measured in its own worker process, which loads NEST and NumPy but none of the other simulators. Every other backend is measured in the main benchmark process, whose footprint is already 629 MB at the session's first measurement. The measured quantity is the peak resident set size of the whole process, including the Python interpreter and all imported libraries. It is taken from the kernel's high-water mark, reset at the start of each measured interval. At the reference size, then, the figure very largely measures the import cost, not the network.
521: This contradicts figures compiled from vendor documentation and secondary literature (Section 2.3), which show machine-learning-stack simulators with the lowest memory overhead on small networks. The contradiction is real, but the two values measure different things. The published numbers are model-level allocation, while this study measures process-level residency. For a researcher fitting a model on a constrained device, the process-level figure is the relevant one, which is why it is reported here.
522: Processor utilisation at the reference size is measured for all eleven backends and ranges from 100.0% to 794.1%. Eight of the eleven use one core (100.0–104.2%). The three that use more are NEST with two threads (239.5%), NEST with four (376.4%) and Brian2's C++ standalone target (794.1%). Values above 100% mean real parallelism. Across all 660 runs of the session, the median is 100.4%, the middle half lies between 100.0% and 189.1%, and the full range is 57.3% to 3,189.1%. The lowest is a single snnTorch run that took 2.4 times its condition's median, a run in which the process was waiting for part of its interval. The highest is Nengo using all thirty-two logical cores. None of these values is a sampling artefact. An earlier version of this section had to exclude readings in the hundreds of thousands of per cent, and the instrument that produced them has been replaced (Section 4.8).
523: The split between NEST and every other backend at the reference size reflects the process each is measured in, as explained above. It is not a property of the simulator, and it shrinks to irrelevance once the network is large enough to matter.
524: The informative measure is therefore the growth of the footprint across the sweep, not its value at any one size. Here the simulators separate sharply, in the opposite direction to what the reference-size figures alone imply. Across its three thread counts, NEST grows from roughly 91–94 MB at 100 neurons to 886–923 MB at 10,000, an increase of some 796–830 MB or 81–85 KB per neuron (growth divided by the 10,000 neurons of the largest network, the convention used throughout). Nengo grows most, from 641 to 2,204 MB, or 160 KB per neuron. snnTorch and SpikingJelly grow by 382 and 383 megabytes respectively, close to 39 kilobytes per neuron. Brian2 barely grows: its NumPy target goes from 629 to 642 megabytes across the whole sweep, 1.32 kilobytes per neuron, and its Cython target 0.45.
525: This ordering is the reverse of what a single-size measurement would support. In Experiment 1, SpikingJelly has the largest footprint of any simulator at 692 MB at one hundred neurons, and NEST the smallest at 91–94 MB across its three thread counts. On that evidence alone, NEST looks like the most memory-efficient simulator studied. Over the sweep the ordering is almost exactly inverted. Brian2's simulating targets add the least per neuron (0.45 and 1.32 kilobytes). NEST, the smallest footprint of any simulator at one hundred neurons, adds 81–85 kilobytes. This is second only to Nengo's 160, and 62 to 65 times Brian2's NumPy target. Both statements come from the same data set. One describes the network being simulated; the other describes what happened to be loaded into the process when the sample was taken.
526: The NEST result is not a bug. NEST can perform the cortical-scale simulations reported in the literature ⟦C1:[50]⟧ because it allocates its kernel structures for the network it is given. Its small footprint at one hundred neurons is the flip side of that same decision, since a network this small needs very little kernel state. The measurement shows that choosing between NEST and Brian2 is a choice about network size, not about which simulator is better engineered. This is the conditional guidance the dashboard's selection guide is designed to convey.
527: Runtime alone also hides processor utilisation, which the corrected instrument measures for every configuration at every size. NEST's utilisation follows its configured thread count almost exactly: 100–101% with one thread, 200–224% with two and 392–485% with four across the sweep. Nengo uses one core up to five hundred neurons (101–100%). From one thousand upwards it uses 3,088–3,173%, about thirty-one of the thirty-two logical cores, because of its multi-threaded linear algebra. SpikingJelly peaks at mid-sized networks (676% at five hundred neurons, 513% at one thousand) and falls back towards one core at ten thousand (128%). snnTorch, the Brian2 NumPy and Cython targets and both NumPy controls stay within ten per cent of one core throughout. Brian2's C++ standalone target keeps about eight cores busy (790–799%) at every size, counted across its compiler and binary processes (Section 4.7). An earlier version of this chapter reported that target at 5.3 per cent and NEST as unmeasurable at the reference size. Both statements came from the defective instrument and are withdrawn. The fastest configurations do not always recruit more cores. At one hundred neurons the fastest simulator configuration, NEST with four threads, uses 3.8 cores to finish 10% sooner than NEST with one, a difference Section 4.3 cannot separate from noise. At ten thousand, however, the two fastest simulator configurations (Brian2's NumPy and Cython targets) use one core each, while Nengo uses 31.7 and is slowest of all. The comparison is fair in that each simulator was configured as its documentation recommends, but not in the sense of equal resources. That distinction carries over to equation (3.8), where utilisation is a multiplicand and not an incidental observation.
528: NEST's three thread counts deserve separate comment, because their ordering does not follow what thread count alone would suggest. At the reference size the three are within noise of each other: 2.367, 2.158 and 2.120 ms for one, two and four threads, with none separated from another after Holm correction. At the largest measured network, two and four threads are indistinguishable (0.498 s and 0.504 s here; in the twin session four threads were faster, 0.463 s against 0.497 s). Both beat one thread (0.681 s) by about 26 per cent. The four-thread configuration uses twice the processor time of the two-thread one to reach the same wall-clock time. On this machine, then, going from two threads to four buys nothing at this size except a larger energy proxy. The return on threads also depends on network size: at five hundred and one thousand neurons, four threads took 14.5% and 14.7% less time than two. A reader who assumes threads scale throughput linearly would be wrong at every size measured here. Why the fourth thread stops paying at ten thousand neurons was not measured.
530: Each simulator was trained with its own native learning mechanism, as described in Section 3.7. The experiment compares cost, not accuracy. Every simulator and backend in this campaign received the same training and test budget: 6,000 training images and 1,000 test images, over three epochs. There was one required exception. Nengo's closed-form decoder solve has no epoch, so its figure is the cost of one solve over the same 6,000 images. Table 4.4 shows what was run and what resulted under that common budget. Table 4.5 gives the measured cost per image of each rule, extrapolates it to the standard reference configuration of 60,000 training and 10,000 test images over ten epochs, and sets that projection beside the measured cost of the full run, executed for all nine backends after the fixed-budget campaign closed. The fixed-budget rows make the cross-simulator comparison controlled; the full-budget rows are what the specification asks for (Section 3.7).
532: The budget column is the same for every row except Nengo's. Fixing the budget isolates cost per epoch and accuracy as the quantities compared, so the budget itself need not be read as a variable. The energy column is listed as not measured throughout. This is a limitation of the executed experiment, not of the design in Section 3.7. The training path timed each adapter's per-epoch work with a wall-clock timer but did not run the utilisation or memory instruments. So neither processor utilisation (a multiplicative term in the proxy) nor peak memory was observed during training, and an energy figure built on an assumed utilisation would restate runtime instead of estimating energy. Measuring them now would mean repeating the training runs with the instruments attached. The full-budget campaign alone occupied this laptop for seven days and twenty hours of wall-clock time by its own log (12 to 20 September), which is why it was not repeated. The corresponding measured quantity here is cost per epoch, which both campaigns timed correctly. Section 4.8 describes the placeholder memory value that the training rows once carried.
534: Two things separate the nine rows, and neither is implementation quality. The first is the class of learning rule, which determines what accuracy is achievable at all. The second is cost per image, which determines what a given budget costs to run. Table 4.5 isolates the second, since it is the quantity the experiment actually compared. It also explains why, at the same fixed budget, the training times in Table 4.4 span more than three orders of magnitude: 0.87 seconds for Nengo's one solve against 1,606.18 seconds for Brian2's C++ standalone target.
535: The projection is computed from measured per-image cost, not a fitted curve, for the reasons given in Section 3.7. The full reference configuration costs seconds for some of the nine rows and most of two days for others. Table 4.5 sets projection and execution side by side so that the projection can be judged instead of trusted.
537: Cost per image of each learning rule and backend, and the cost of the full reference specification, projected from it and then measured by executing it. The budget in Table 4.4 is now constant across rows. This projection, not the budget column, shows where the real cost differences between learning rules lie.
539: Setting the projection beside the execution shows where per-image extrapolation can be trusted. For NEST it is accurate to within 8 per cent at every thread count, and the three ratios fall on both sides of unity. The cost of that rule really is one simulation call per image, so multiplying a per-image figure by the image count is the right model. The measured per-image cost also barely moves between budgets. For the two gradient libraries the projection overestimates by about half again, and for Nengo's closed-form solve by a factor of two and a half. In both cases part of the per-image cost measured at the smaller budget is fixed overhead that does not recur: snnTorch costs 2.416 milliseconds per image at 6,000 images and 1.535 at 60,000. The projection is therefore not a safe upper bound. For the plasticity rules it errs in both directions, between 0.84 and 1.16 times the measured cost. For Brian2 / Cython and NEST / 1 thread the measured cost exceeds the projection, by 19 per cent in the worst case, while the remaining plasticity backends fall between 0.98 and 1.16. These are the expensive rules, where the number decides whether a run is attempted at all. There, a projection built from per-image cost at a small budget should be read as an estimate with an error of roughly a fifth either way, not as a ceiling.
540: The methodological point goes beyond these five tools. Section 2.2 argued on theoretical grounds that the final accuracy of different learning rules cannot be compared directly. The measured result imposes a stricter constraint. The rules differ by orders of magnitude in sample efficiency and in cost per sample, so any study comparing accuracy across these paradigms must budget compute for the slowest rule, not the fastest. Because this campaign fixes the budget, that constraint is directly visible: the same 6,000/1,000 budget takes under a second for Nengo and almost twenty-seven minutes for Brian2's C++ standalone target. That cost is why this thesis reports training time as the comparable quantity and treats accuracy as a per-configuration outcome at a stated, now-equal budget.
541: The results clearly separate simulators whose learning rules converged from those whose rules diverged, and the division follows rule class, not implementation quality. The two surrogate-gradient libraries reach the highest accuracies: SpikingJelly 94.10 per cent on the held-out set and snnTorch 93.20 per cent. Both were trained on the same 6,000 images for three epochs at a hidden width of 256, with an identical procedure: rate-coded Poisson input over a 25-millisecond window, spike-count readout as logits, and Adam optimization. Landing within one percentage point of each other is the expected result, and more reassuring than interesting. It shows that the harness measures the procedure, not incidental differences between two implementations of it. Given their similar accuracy, the more informative comparison is cost: SpikingJelly takes 13.79 seconds per epoch against 14.50 for snnTorch.
542: Nengo scores 85.50 per cent by a route that is not comparable in kind. The Neural Engineering Framework solves for the decoding weights in one closed-form least-squares step, with no epoch, no gradient and no iteration. The reported 0.87 seconds is the cost of that single solve against the same 6,000 training examples. It is by far the cheapest route to a working classifier in this study. It also has the lowest ceiling of the rules that converge at all, since accuracy is limited by how well an ensemble of the given width can represent a 784-dimensional space. Both facts are properties of the method and matter for simulator choice. Neither is captured by putting 85.50 in a column next to 94.10.
543: Raising the budget separates the rules by what limits them. The two surrogate-gradient libraries gain three to four percentage points, with SpikingJelly reaching 97.46 per cent and snnTorch 97.24. They also converge on each other: 0.22 points apart at the full budget against 0.90 at the reduced one. This is further evidence that the harness measures the shared procedure and not two implementations of it. Nengo does not move at all (85.44 against 85.50). That is expected for a closed-form solve, whose ceiling depends on how well an ensemble of a given width can represent a 784-dimensional space, not on how many examples it sees. The plasticity rules gain between 0.82 and 2.21 points. No configuration exceeds the ten per cent chance level, though the closest now sits within measurement noise of it. One table therefore shows three different limits: sample efficiency for the gradient rules, representational capacity for the decoder solve, and a missing homeostatic mechanism for the plasticity rules.
544: The unsupervised rules did not converge, and the thesis reports this instead of leaving it out. Across its three thread counts NEST scores between 7.40 and 7.50 per cent, and Brian2 scores between 7.70 and 7.80 per cent across its three backends. Chance level on ten classes is 10 per cent, so every configuration of both is at or below chance. The cause is known and recorded in the condition logs, not inferred afterwards. Unsupervised spike-timing-dependent plasticity has no mechanism for symmetry breaking. All hidden neurons see the same input under the same update rule and converge to the same receptive field. The labeling pass assigns most of them to one class, and that class wins every test presentation. The effect grows stronger, not weaker, in later epochs. The implementation follows a published procedure that provides three mechanisms not implemented here. These are lateral inhibition to enforce competition, an adaptive threshold to stop any neuron dominating, and weight normalization so that neurons compete on the shape of a receptive field and not its magnitude. That procedure also uses a much larger sample budget ⟦C1:[26]⟧, ⟦C2:[28]⟧, ⟦C3:[29]⟧. The mechanisms and the budget should be considered separately. The budget alone was tested here by executing the full reference configuration, which raises accuracy by only 0.82 to 2.21 percentage points (see below). What these rows lack is the mechanisms, not the budget.
545: The correct reading of these six rows is that they measure the absence of those mechanisms. They do not measure the capability of NEST or Brian2, nor differences between thread counts or code-generation backends. Each of these agrees with the others in its own family to within 0.31 of a percentage point. An earlier version of this paragraph also named the size of the sample budget as a cause. That explanation has since been tested and can be discarded. Re-running the same configurations at the full reference budget of 60,000 training images over ten epochs moves NEST from 7.40–7.50 per cent to 8.32–8.41 per cent and Brian2 from 7.70–7.80 per cent to 9.60–9.91 per cent. The ordering among thread counts and code-generation backends stays unchanged. The gain from extra data is uneven: NEST gains 0.82 to 0.99 points and Brian2 1.80 to 2.21. Ten times the sample budget is therefore worth between 0.82 and 2.21 percentage points depending on the rule. Both simulators implement spike-timing-dependent plasticity correctly. What is missing is the surrounding architecture that makes the rule discriminative, and a larger budget does not substitute for it. The dashboard notes this explicitly next to the affected rows and prints the sample budget each row actually used in the same table. An accuracy figure reported without its budget invites exactly the misreading these rows would otherwise produce.
546: The broader methodological point is that accuracy is not comparable across learning rules, whereas cost per epoch is. The fixed-budget rows of Table 4.4 capture a snapshot of two convergence curves with different shapes, taken at three epochs for surrogate-gradient and plasticity rules alike. The full-budget rows add a second snapshot of the same two curves at ten epochs. Epoch count here is a coordinate on the horizontal axis, not a controlled variable. This is why, as Section 3.7 sets out, Experiment 2 aims at the cost of learning and not its quality, and why the accuracy column always appears with the conditions that generated it.
548: Brian2’s C++ standalone target took 1.6782 s for N = 100 and 1.6911 s for N = 10,000, giving k = +0.001 with R-squared = 0.013. This runtime does not respond at all to a hundredfold change in network size, which no simulator's workload does. Mean processor utilization over the same sweep stays between 790 and 799 per cent, or about eight cores busy throughout. Its two interpreted siblings, at one core, move in the direction a simulator's runtime should, but only weakly. Brian2 / NumPy moves from 0.1291 s to 0.1466 s over the same hundredfold change (k = +0.023, R-squared = 0.688), and Brian2 / Cython from 0.1337 s to 0.1652 s (k = +0.048, R-squared = 0.330). Cython's weaker fit reflects the near-flat, noise-dominated runtime seen in its cross-size times in Table 4.3.
549: A backend whose runtime does not depend on problem size is not measuring problem size. Brian2’s standalone devices regenerate and recompile the source code on each invocation, because the device must be reinitialized between runs so that the second run does not silently reuse the first build. The measured interval is therefore dominated by the compiler, not the simulation, and processor utilisation is consistent with that. Each run uses about eight cores' worth of processor time, counted across the Python process and the build and binary processes it starts, against one core for the targets that simulate in the Python process. How that time divides between compiling and running was not measured. An earlier version of this section read the same target's utilisation as five per cent and inferred a process waiting on its tool-chain. That reading counted only the parent Python process, not the child processes doing the work, and is withdrawn (Section 4.8).
550: The implication for benchmarking methodology is worth carrying forward, and it applies far beyond Brian2. Chapter 3 specifies discarded warmup runs precisely so that first-run compilation is excluded from the reported figure. That protocol assumes a single compilation. If a backend recompiles on every run, no number of warmup runs can prevent this, and the protocol silently reports compiler throughput as simulator throughput. We therefore report the pure backends as capability results, since they compile and run correctly, and exclude them from the runtime comparison. Placing a compile-dominated number next to a measured simulation time would compare a compiler with a simulator.
552: This campaign found five defects in the harness and the adapters, and three of them invalidate results reported in earlier drafts of this work. They are reported here in the results chapter, not in an appendix, because a benchmark is only as trustworthy as its instruments. A reader is entitled to know what was wrong with these instruments and when.
555: A fifth defect belongs with the four above, and it was found only by running the experiment at full size. The harness runs each NEST training attempt in a disposable subprocess, because NEST 3.10.0 crashed the whole process after a small number of kernel resets on this machine. It also caps the number of attempts. The cap was two hundred, and each attempt ends at a sixty-second deadline whether or not anything has gone wrong, so total work was capped at three hours and twenty minutes. At the fixed budget of Table 4.4, the four-thread configuration needs about nine minutes of that ceiling, or one twentieth of it. That is why the limit was never reached in the first campaign. At the full reference budget, the same configuration needs just under four hours once the labelling and test passes are counted alongside the ten epochs, so the ceiling stops it before it finishes. It stopped during the labelling pass, after completing all ten training epochs. The single-thread configuration was stopped by the same cap; the two-thread configuration was not. The harness then reported that subprocess isolation could not complete training for that backend after two hundred worker attempts. The message names NEST, and a reader would reasonably conclude that NEST had failed. In fact nothing had failed except the instrument's own retry budget. That budget had been sized against the old sample count and never revisited when the sample count changed. The ceiling was raised to a thousand attempts of five minutes, and the three NEST configurations then completed normally. The general form of this defect applies beyond NEST. A resilience mechanism whose limits are tuned to one problem size will, at a larger size, fail in a way that blames the system under test instead of the measuring apparatus.
556: One more change was tried and rejected. A negative result on one's own optimization is as informative as a positive one. Brian2's training path was switched from the interpreted code-generation target to the compiled one in the hope of a speed-up, but it timed slower (0.65 seconds per image against 0.32). Each image is a separate simulation call over a short window, so per-call setup dominates and the compiled inner loop never runs long enough to repay its cost. The change was rolled back.
557: The seven defects in results recording and reporting were found while building the dashboard and finalising this chapter, not during the original campaign. The first four did not affect the underlying measurements, only the figures presented from them. The fifth and sixth are the exceptions, because each caused a value that was never measured to be stored as though it had been. The seventh again affected presentation only. This class of error comes from how results are stored, aggregated or analysed, not from how they were taken. It is invisible in the final figures, which is exactly why it is the kind most likely to survive into a published table.
558: The first is duplicate condition records. The results database is append-only by design: running a simulator again writes new rows instead of overwriting existing ones. This makes a partial re-run safe after an interruption and preserves full provenance across sessions. The price is that a condition measured several times appears several times. Here the Brian2 Cython target was measured twice for calibration, giving three separate rows per condition. A chart drawn directly from the table showed that backend as three overlapping series with slightly different values, and any aggregate across the table weighted it three times. The remedy is that the data layer answers every query with the most recent row for each simulator/backend/task/size/phase combination. Rows are ordered by insertion order, not timestamp, because two rows written in the same second share a timestamp and would otherwise be ordered arbitrarily. The obsolete rows remain in the database for audit; they are excluded from presentation, not deleted.
559: The second is whether compile-heavy backends are eligible for summary rankings. The Brian2 standalone target's reported time is dominated by a C++ toolchain, not by simulation (Section 4.7). This has three consequences, each misleading on its own. At the reference size it is an order of magnitude slower than the slowest simulating backend in the study. When scaled, it gives an exponent indistinguishable from zero. And since the simulation runs in a separate compiled binary, the process whose memory is measured is not the one holding the network. Before the safeguard, this backend held the top spot for both flattest scaling and lowest peak memory, so an artifact won two of the four summary figures.
560: The solution is a single, uniform eligibility rule. Rows marked compile-dominated, and rows belonging to the plain reference implementation, are left out of every summary ranking. They remain fully present in every chart, table and export, labelled as Section 3.12 describes. This is a deliberate, conservative choice. Removing the rows outright would have been easier but would have hidden a real finding, since Brian2's standalone behaviour here is exactly what a practitioner choosing a code-generation strategy needs to know. The harness sets the compile-dominated flag at measurement time, from runtime that is large and largely invariant with network size. It is not applied by hand to a backend known in advance to have the property.
561: The third concerns the machine a stored row was measured on, and it struck the study's central control, not its presentation. A partial re-run was once made on a different computer, and because the database is append-only, those records were written alongside the campaign's. The query layer resolves each condition to its most recently written record, so the newer rows could have silently replaced the campaign's own. Every query is now restricted to an explicit list of run_groups on the LT68 laptop (one list per experiment, identified in Section 4.2), not to whichever record was written last. The 462 excluded condition records named there are the visible trace of that safeguard, kept so the exclusion can be audited. The defect reappeared in a milder form exactly where this predicts. The dashboard's data-access layer restricted queries to the campaign's machine identifier but not, at first, to the same two run_groups. So twelve rows from an unrelated same-machine recalibration silently won over the campaign's own Brian2/NumPy measurements in the live interface, even after the analysis script had been corrected. Both now read the same explicit run_group lists instead of deriving them again. The lesson generalizes: an append-only store is the right design for a benchmark, since it makes partial re-runs safe. But it shifts the burden of defining a campaign onto every query layer that reads the store, not just the first one fixed.
562: The fourth is silent degradation of the statistics pipeline when an optional dependency is missing. The analysis script imports SciPy inside a try/except. Instead of raising, it falls back to a null statistics object so the harness can run without SciPy. Every downstream Shapiro-Wilk, Levene, Welch-ANOVA, Welch pairwise and correlation call is then skipped rather than computed. During an environment migration, the interpreter running analyse.py lacked SciPy for a while. The script ran without error and produced its usual two output files, but they omitted the entire statistical layer of Section 3.10. Nothing in the console output, ANALYSIS.md or analysis.json marked that run as different, because a guarded skip and a true absence of signal look identical downstream. The pipeline flagged nothing; it was caught only by cross-checking against a new run with SciPy confirmed importable. The guard itself is kept as a reasonable defense against SciPy being unavailable. Analysis now runs in an environment verified to have every adapter's dependency, with that import asserted before invocation, so a missing dependency fails loudly instead of silently.
564: The fifth is a value reported as measured that was not measured. It is the most serious of the seven: it entered the stored data rather than just its presentation, and its first remedy was itself defective. A background thread sampled processor utilization every five milliseconds. A region with no sample was stored as a literal one hundred per cent, in 168 of 669 runs of the original campaign. The first remedy, on 27 August, withdrew those values and made the harness difference the process CPU-time counters across the measured region. Both halves proved insufficient. Native simulator code that holds Python's global interpreter lock prevents the sampling thread from running at all, so the failure was not limited to short regions. A 0.48-second NEST simulation received no sample, and 181 of the 501 remaining runs received fewer than a quarter of the samples their duration implies. The samples that did arrive, each a difference of clock ticks over a few milliseconds, read anything up to 388,844 per cent. The counters used by the remedy advance in ten-millisecond ticks on Linux, so a region lasting about a millisecond reads either zero or around a thousand per cent. In the September campaign, every one of the 291 regions shorter than 50 milliseconds has a CPU time that is an exact multiple of ten milliseconds. Neither campaign's utilization, and so neither campaign's energy proxy, was a measurement. Runtime, timed separately by a high-resolution clock, was never affected. Nor were memory, spike counts or accuracy, although the memory sampler shared the same starved thread and could miss a short-lived peak. The instrument now reads the kernel's per-process CPU clock, which the scheduler keeps in nanoseconds for every thread and which needs no thread scheduled to observe it. It adds the processor time of child processes the region waits for, and reads peak memory from the kernel's high-water mark, reset at the start of each region. No sampling thread runs during a measurement at all. Before every campaign it is now checked against loads whose answer is known. On this laptop it read 100.5% for a one-millisecond busy loop, where the original sampler read a median of 0% and a maximum of 25,056%. It read 195% for two threads outside the interpreter lock and, measured alone as the benchmark uses it, a median of 0.1–1.3% while sleeping. It registered 199 MB of a 200 MB allocation that existed for a fraction of a second. Experiments 1 and 3 were then measured again under the identical protocol on 20 September. Every inference and scalability figure in this chapter comes from that session, and every one of its 660 runs carries a utilization reading. The August campaign's utilization values were withdrawn from the database and its runtimes kept as a replication (Section 4.4). No run was deleted. The repair was only possible because Section 3.13 stores every individual run rather than a summary.
565: The sixth is similar, in a smaller place. The training path does not run the memory instrument. Yet it wrote a peak memory of 0.0 MB and a memory change of 0.0 MB into every training row as placeholders, in 26 condition records and 29 runs of the results database. A zero is a value, and neither a reader nor a query can tell it apart from an absence. The placeholders are now stored as missing, the harness writes missing rather than zero, and Section 4.6 states that training memory was not measured.
566: The seventh was found while re-checking the interface against the tables for this revision. The harness stores training cost already divided per epoch, and the dashboard's training page divided it by the epoch count again. Every training cost it displayed was therefore a third (fixed budget) or a tenth (full budget) of the figure in Table 4.4. Nengo's single solve was shown at a third of its measured time. The thesis tables read the stored value directly and were never affected; the interface now does the same.
567: The first four defects share a structure. The measurements and the storage were correct; the error crept in only where stored measurements were converted into a displayed figure or reported statistic. The fifth and sixth are the instructive counter-examples. There the storage itself was wrong, and no care at the presentation layer could have saved it, since a benchmark reporting only aggregates cannot expose a defect in the aggregate. The fifth also shows that a remedy needs the same scrutiny as the defect: the counter-based fix passed every check except the one that mattered, a test against a load whose answer is known. Seven safeguards were adopted. Duplicates are resolved at query time, every query is restricted to explicitly listed run_groups, and incomparable rows are flagged at measurement time. A statistical dependency is asserted rather than silently degraded, and every individual run is retained. Every figure is computed in one shared layer used by both thesis and interface. Every instrument is tested against known loads before it is trusted. They are a contribution to benchmarking practice in their own right, because each was adopted in response to a defect that had already produced a wrong figure.
569: The energy proxy returns a value in joules for every run measured. Section 3.9 set out a three-part validation, reported here. The aim is to find out exactly what the proxy is good for. The answer is that it ranks reliably, but it estimates rather than measures.
570: The first question is whether the proxy tracks the amount of work. Table 4.7 gives the Spearman rank correlation between the proxy and the analytically derived synaptic operation count over the size sweep, calculated separately for each simulator. The synaptic operation count depends only on the network specification each simulator was told to construct. It is therefore a simulator-independent reference, not an additional metric.
572: One row per backend. Every backend has a measured energy value at all five sizes, so each coefficient is calculated over five points. With five points, the smallest attainable exact p-value is 0.017.
576: (One plot per simulator, both axes on a log scale. Faceting instead of a multi-colored scatter is intentional. Separating the simulators lets each relationship be read on its own and avoids a chart where a color-blind reader cannot tell the series apart.)
577: The proxy increases monotonically with the theoretical workload for 8 of the eleven backends, at rho = +1.000 each: NEST's three thread counts, Nengo, snnTorch, SpikingJelly and both NumPy controls. The three Brian2 targets are the exceptions. NumPy agrees strongly but not perfectly (rho = +0.900, p = 0.083) and Cython weakly (rho = +0.700, p = 0.233). The C++ standalone target does not agree at all (rho = -0.400, p = 0.517), as expected for a backend whose runtime does not scale with network size. This answers RQ2. The proxy is ordinal, and it does not invert the ordering of workloads for any backend whose runtime is driven by simulation rather than by fixed overhead or compilation. A selection instrument needs exactly this. Its agreement is stronger than an earlier version of this section reported, because the utilisation values behind that version were partly noise. The accuracy of the joule values is left to the physical comparison in Section 6.5.
578: The second question is how much of the proxy is just runtime in other units. A regression of log energy on log runtime for all 660 runs of the corrected session gives a slope of 1.141, R-squared = 0.911. The formula's only other term, processor utilisation, has a median of 100.4% over those runs. The middle half lies between 100.0% and 189.1%, the full range 57.3% to 3,189.1%; no reading is excluded.
579: So, with utilisation measured correctly, the proxy is mostly runtime in other units: runtime alone explains 91% of the variance in log energy. An earlier version of this section reported 42% and concluded that utilisation was doing substantial independent work. The defective utilisation values produced that conclusion, because their noise looked like independent information, and it is withdrawn. The remaining variance is real and sits largely where utilisation departs from one core: NEST's thread counts, Nengo's linear algebra from one thousand neurons upwards, SpikingJelly's mid-sized runs and Brian2's parallel compiler. Six configurations stay within ten per cent of one core at every size: Brian2's NumPy and Cython targets, NEST with one thread, snnTorch and both NumPy controls. For these the proxy is runtime multiplied by a near-constant and adds almost nothing to it.
580: The third question changes the proxy's own constants. Thermal design power was varied by ±30% and the utilisation exponent between 0.8 and 1.2. Each of the nine resulting orderings was compared with the nominal ordering by Kendall's tau at N = 10,000, the reference size of Experiment 4, where all eleven backends are ranked. Six of the nine give 1.000 agreement and the other three 0.964. Thermal design power has no effect at all. This is structural, not just empirical: it enters the formula as a constant multiplier, so it cannot reorder anything. The only change comes from the utilisation exponent, and only at the top of its range. There the two closest backends in the nominal ordering, NEST with two threads and SpikingJelly, switch places. The ordering is therefore robust to large errors in these untestable constants, which makes the proxy usable for simulator selection even without validated absolute values.
581: In short, RQ2 is answered within its stated scope. The proxy keeps the ordering of workloads by theoretical cost for every backend whose runtime follows the workload, and that ordering is robust to substantial errors in its own parameters. A selection instrument needs this, since a reader acts on the ordering rather than on the joule value. On this hardware the proxy adds information to runtime only where a simulator uses more than one core, which is also where it matters most. It does not measure joules, and this thesis never claims it does. The physical power-meter comparison that would make it quantitative is specified in Section 6.5.
583: Experiment 4 tests whether the ordering above is a property of the simulators or of two settings every benchmark in this field chooses silently. These are the network size at which the comparison is reported and the metric used to rank it. It uses the instrument set out in Section 3.11: the ordering is recomputed under a changed setting, and its agreement with the reference ordering is reported as Kendall's tau-b over the eleven backends measured at every size. Everything comes from the existing scalability sweep, with no new measurement. No p-value accompanies the coefficients, because with eleven items a significance test has little power, and the rank movements visible in Figure 4.4 are the substantive finding.
586: (Calculated as Kendall's tau-b. A bar at 1.0 is an ordering identical to the reference. In the three left bars, between 31 and 38 per cent of the ordered pairs are reversed relative to it.)
588: Measured by Kendall's tau-b. Size rows are compared with the runtime ordering at the largest measured network, metric rows with the runtime ordering at the same size. A value of 1.000 means the order is the same.
592: (Largest measured network size. The reference is runtime against itself. A value of zero or below means the ordering holds no information about the runtime ordering.)
593: This methodological addition lets the ordering be presented as a finding rather than an observation. Every published comparison of these tools reviewed in Chapter 2 stops at the ordering without testing it against the arbitrary choices behind it.
594: The first question is whether the ordering depends on the network size at which it is measured. The reference is the ordering by median runtime at N=10 000. Agreement at each smaller size is tau=0.273 for N=100, tau=0.236 for N=500, tau=0.382 for N=1 000, and tau=0.818 for N=5 000. The pattern is clear, and it is this chapter's most important result. At the three smallest sizes the ordering has little in common with the ordering at the largest. Agreement is weakest at N = 500, not at the smallest size. Only at N = 5 000 does the ranking regain most of its agreement with the full sweep, and even there some ordered pairs still disagree. The low agreement at small sizes appears in each of the four sessions that measured the sweep, with agreement at N = 100 between 0.200 and 0.273 (Section 4.4). A benchmark that stopped short of five thousand neurons would have published an ordering sharing only slightly more ordered pairs with the ten-thousand ordering than chance would.
595: The fitted exponents behind the metric comparison that follows come from the same session and are given here to check the rank correlation against them. Ordered by exponent, the values are: Nengo / reference k = +1.550, NEST / 1 thread k = +1.199, NEST / 4 threads k = +1.195, NEST / 2 threads k = +1.151, SpikingJelly / CPU k = +1.026. They continue with the scalar NumPy control k = +0.993, snnTorch / CPU k = +0.895, the vectorized NumPy control k = +0.735, Brian2 / Cython k = +0.048, Brian2 / NumPy k = +0.023 and Brian2 / C++ standalone k = +0.001. All three Brian2 backends sit at the bottom of that ordering. Two of them, the NumPy and Cython targets, are also near the top of the runtime ordering at the reference size, and supply most of the agreement there is. Without them the coefficient falls to 0.056. The compile-dominated target, flat but slow, pulls it down (without it, 0.467).
596: Put simply, a benchmark that ranked simulators on one small network would recommend a different simulator from one that used a large network. The instrument, machine and model would be the same. This is not a theoretical threat. It is the common reporting convention in the comparative literature reviewed in Chapter 2. There, a single network size is the norm, and it is typically small enough to finish quickly. The finding also helps explain why the dashboard attaches its simulator-selection guidance to the scalability sweep rather than the inference figure. It is also why the inference view puts the network size in its own heading, not in a caption.
597: The second question is whether the ordering depends on the metric used. The reference is the runtime ordering at the largest size. Ordering the same backends by the energy proxy gives tau = 0.782, by peak memory tau = +0.418, and by fitted scaling exponent tau = 0.236. The energy result is the strongest of the three because the proxy is largely rescaled runtime for most backends (Section 4.9). Every pair it reorders involves NEST with two or four threads, whose extra cores do not buy proportionally shorter runs. Speed and memory economy are moderately associated rather than opposed. Brian2's simulating targets are among both the fastest and the most frugal at the largest network, and Nengo is both the slowest and the largest at N = 10 000. But the association is far too weak to predict one from the other. Section 4.5 is the place to read the mechanism, not the correlation coefficient.
598: The scaling-exponent result is also important, and less intuitive. The ordering by exponent is weakly associated with the runtime ordering, at tau = 0.236. This is the weakest of the three metric comparisons. It is driven largely by Brian2's NumPy and Cython targets, which are among both the fastest and the flattest. Without those two the coefficient is 0.056, so there is no general tendency for fast configurations to scale flatly. How fast a simulator is at one network size still says little about how its cost grows as the network scales. Nengo is the clearest counter-example: fast enough at N = 100 to rank fifth on runtime, yet the steepest backend measured. These remain two largely independent questions. A practitioner who answers the second by measuring the first has not approximated the answer; they have substituted a weakly related one.
599: Together, the two tests support one conclusion, stated here as the answer to the sensitivity question rather than left implicit. A single-size, single-metric benchmark result is not a recommendation about a simulator. It is a recommendation of a metric at a size, and it changes whenever either one changes. This does not make the measurements unreliable. The coefficients of variation reported throughout Chapter 4 are low, and the individual runs behind every median are kept and shown. But a recommendation drawn from them must state the conditions under which it holds. The dashboard's selection guidance does exactly that, which is why it is conditional and not a ranking.
600: The third test addresses Objective O2 directly: estimating the rank correlation between the utilization-weighted energy proxy and an EFLOP-based estimate.
