Across all 55 scalability conditions of the session, Spearman’s rho between the two is 0.645 over 55 paired observations, a strong positive agreement. An earlier version of this section gave 0.716 over 50 observations. That figure no longer followed from the stored data after the August repair, and it rested on the defective utilisation values in any case, so it is replaced. But the coefficient alone hides what the comparison showed. The more significant finding is structural, not numerical.
601: The EFLOP metric gives exactly one value for each simulator at any fixed network size: at N = 10 000 all eleven backends have the same effective operation count. This is the expected behavior for the metric as defined by Narduzzi et al. ⟦C1:[21]⟧, which counts the operations the network model performs. The model is the same across simulators by construction, and that identity is what makes the comparison in this thesis valid in the first place. EFLOP therefore cannot discriminate between simulators at a fixed size. The reported rank correlation of 0.645 is driven by variation across network sizes, not across implementations.
602: This is a finding about the instrument, not a flaw in its implementation, and it bears directly on the second research question. By definition, an operation-count proxy is portable between machines because it ignores what the machine did. It ignores this because it counts the model, not the execution. It is the better instrument for comparing the same model across hardware. It cannot separate different implementations of the same model on one machine, which is the question this study asks. The two proxies are therefore reported side by side rather than one replacing the other. This limitation is noted on the panel that displays the correlation, not in a footnote. This follows Henderson et al., whose systematic-reporting framework for machine-learning energy costs argues for reporting an energy estimate with its assumptions, not as a single opaque number.
604: Section 4.10 answers RQ1 in full. The five simulators separate cleanly on every dimension measured in Sections 4.3-4.7, but that separation is not one stable ordering. Agreement with the N = 10 000 reference ordering falls to tau = 0.236 at N = 500 and recovers only to tau = 0.818 by N = 5 000. Low agreement at the small sizes appears in every one of four measurement sessions. The ordering shifts again under an alternative ranking metric (tau = 0.782 against the energy proxy, +0.418 against peak memory, 0.236 against the fitted scaling exponent). On this single controlled platform, RQ1 is answered in both its halves. These are how the simulators compare, and whether that comparison holds under the network sizes and metrics a reader might choose.
605: RQ2 asks how valid a runtime-based energy proxy is against the EFLOP metric, by Spearman rank correlation. Section 4.10's third test gives Spearman's rho = 0.645 across the 55 paired observations of the session. That correlation reflects network size, not implementation (Section 4.10). Per backend (Section 4.9), the proxy follows the workload for every configuration whose runtime is driven by simulation, keeps its ordering under substantial error in its own constants, and adds information to runtime only where a simulator uses several cores. Its practical value is therefore ordinal, which is the property a simulator-selection instrument needs, not the property a wattmeter would supply. Physical validation against measured power is specified as future work in Section 6.5.
606: RQ3 asks how a dashboard can be designed to let a researcher filter and compare results by simulator, backend and experiment type. Chapter 5 answers it with a working instrument and a design finding: a hardware axis cannot express this comparison, so the dashboard is organized around a backend axis (Section 3.12). Every view recomputes from the backends a reader selects (Section 5.2).
608: The measurements come from a single laptop with thirty-two logical cores, so absolute runtimes do not transfer to any other machine (Section 3.4). The thread-parallel setups are affected in the opposite direction to a constrained machine. NEST gains a real benefit from a second thread at the largest network size and none from four (Section 4.5). That pattern is a property of this specific core count, cache topology and WSL2 scheduler. It does not show how the same configuration would scale with more or fewer cores, a native Linux kernel or different memory bandwidth per core. It should not be generalized beyond the hardware it was measured on.
609: The statistical limits stated in Section 3.10 apply: repeats within a condition are not independent, so the measured range is within-session variability only, and five is a small sample, with one of eleven backends failing the Shapiro-Wilk test. The pairwise Welch tests in Section 4.3 carry that caveat. Variability between sessions was measured separately (Section 4.4); it is larger for absolute times, though not for orderings.
610: The equivalence check between the simulator implementations compares firing rates and output agreement. It does not check that the simulators implement the same equations with the same numerical method, and two implementations can agree on firing rate while using different solvers. Published commentary on an apparent runtime discrepancy, which turned out to be one simulator silently using a different integration scheme, indicates this residual risk is real, not theoretical.
611: The training results carry two more limitations. Every training-capable backend received the same budget, which removes the differing-budget confound of the earlier campaign's equivalent measurement. But equalising images and epochs does not make a closed-form solve, surrogate-gradient backpropagation and unsupervised plasticity comparable, for the reasons Section 4.6 sets out. The accuracies therefore remain per-configuration outcomes at a now-common budget, not a like-for-like comparison. The presentation window is also measurably too short for the spike-timing-dependent-plasticity simulators, as Table 4.6 shows, so their accuracy figures are conditional on that setting. A third belongs with them: processor utilisation, peak memory and therefore the energy proxy were not observed during training, for the reason Section 4.6 gives, so Experiment 2 reports cost as time only.
612: Finally, execution was measured on a single hardware platform. This design choice, argued for in Section 3.4, makes the chapter's comparisons attributable to the simulators rather than the machines they ran on. Its claims are therefore restricted to processor-based execution. The capability probe in Appendix B implements and exercises the harness's CUDA, ROCm and Metal paths; measuring through them is the extension specified in Section 6.5.
614: The chapter found that the speed ordering reverses across the range of network sizes a researcher would reasonably use: Kendall's tau-b between the extremes is 0.273 and falls as low as 0.236; agreement between the extremes is low in every one of four sessions, while orderings re-measured at a fixed size agree closely (Sections 4.4 and 4.10). Some configurations scale their cost with the problem; others are dominated by fixed overhead, and one Brian2 backend measures its own compiler (Section 4.7). The ordering by scaling exponent does not depend on which size is reported, so it can be read as a property of the simulators rather than of the experiment. It is, however, only weakly related to speed at any one size. For backends whose runtime tracks the workload, the energy proxy preserves the ordering of workloads by theoretical cost and is stable under substantial error in its own constants, but it is largely runtime rescaled except where a simulator uses several cores (Section 4.9). Twelve defects were also found and corrected in the measuring and reporting instruments, five in the harness and seven in the recording and reporting layer (Section 4.8). The most serious, in the processor-utilisation instrument, required Experiments 1 and 3 to be measured again.
615: What the chapter does not prove is just as worth saying. It says nothing about GPU performance, many-core scaling, or recurrent or convolutional spiking architectures. Nor does it say which simulator learns better, only how much each costs to run and how that cost scales with the problem.
620: Section 3.12 described the dashboard's design rules and architecture, and Chapter 4 reported the study's findings as a fixed sequence of figures and tables, each built once from the full backend set. This chapter treats the dashboard as the study's second, applied output. It shows how the same measurements look through the interface a reader uses, and states what an interactive view can carry that a printed figure cannot. It closes by honestly assessing how far the prototype goes toward the requirement stated in Section 3.12.
622: Every figure in Chapter 4 was fixed when it was drawn: a stated subset of backends, one snapshot of the results database, printed once. The dashboard reads the identical database, but nothing on its pages is fixed. A simulator selector at the top of every view lets a reader add or remove backends. Every chart, headline figure and one-line finding then recomputes from the rows still selected; no pre-rendered image is swapped in. Figure 5.1 shows the overview page with the default selection. Four headline statistics (fastest inference, lowest peak memory, flattest scaling, best training accuracy) come live from the database, each naming the backend that earns it. De-selecting a backend that holds one of those headlines changes the figure, the backend name and the sentence beneath it in one step. The sentence is generated from the same filtered rows as the number, not typed in beside it. So the design rule in Section 3.12, that nothing is shown that was not computed from what is on screen, applies to the reading experience as well as to the chart.
626: Chapter 4 uses bar and line charts throughout. These suit a ranking or a trend but flatten two other kinds of question the data supports. The dashboard adds three forms, each chosen for the question it answers rather than for variety. A slope chart compares two rankings directly. Figure 5.2 draws each backend's speed rank at the smallest network size on the left and at the largest on the right, joined by a line. A backend that holds its position is a flat line; one that does not is a diagonal. This carries the same information as the rank-agreement statistics in Section 4.10 but shows which individual backends move, not only the aggregate tau.
629: The remaining two forms appear together on the Provenance page (Figure 5.3). A scatter chart plots two measured quantities against each other, one point per backend. Here it plots each backend's measured firing rate against the plain-NumPy reference rate, so a reader sees agreement as distance from a dashed line instead of subtracting two numbers (Figure 5.3, left). A donut chart answers a composition question directly. It shows how many selected backends passed the equivalence check and how many failed, at a glance rather than as a column of pass/fail tags (Figure 5.3, right). None of these three forms changes a number reported in Chapter 4. They change which questions a reader can answer without first doing arithmetic on a table.
633: The honest answer is a qualified one. The dashboard works for the purpose it was built for: letting an examiner or the researcher re-derive a filtered view of the campaign without opening the results database or the appendix tables by hand. All six experiment pages, the overview, the ranked all-simulators page and the about page were exercised against the full backend set during verification. The simulator selector was confirmed to change every chart, table and result line on the page it touches, with zero console errors across all nine routes. This is a real efficiency gain over reading Chapter 4 with a pencil, crossing out rows for backends the reader does not care about.
634: It is not, however, a benchmarking service. The dashboard is read-only by design (Section 3.12), so a reader cannot point it at their own hardware. Its absolute timings transfer to no machine other than the one recorded in Table 3.5, for the reason argued in Section 4.12. Its contribution is presentational, not predictive: it changes how the existing measurements can be read, not what they claim. Its usefulness depends on the question asked of it. For verifying this thesis's own results, it is useful. For choosing a simulator on different hardware without repeating the campaign, it is no more useful than the printed tables.
636: The dashboard reads the same database as Chapter 4 and adds nothing to it. What changes is how a reader can move through it. Every page responds to a live simulator selection. Three chart forms not used in the printed figures (scatter, slope, donut) answer questions that bar and line charts flatten. The result is demonstrably more efficient than the printed page for re-deriving a filtered view of this campaign's own data, but it is not an instrument for measuring anything beyond it.
641: This thesis aims to establish, through controlled measurement, the relative performance of Brian2, NEST, Nengo, snnTorch and SpikingJelly and how far it can be trusted. It also releases the suite and dashboard that make the evidence reproducible and usable. It addressed three gaps identified in Chapter 2. There was no common benchmark spanning all five simulators whose ordering has been tested for stability. There was also no validated energy proxy for commodity hardware, and no interactive means of putting benchmark results into use.
642: All three research questions are answered together with the conditions under which the answers hold. RQ1 was answered on a single hardware platform in both halves. The five simulators separate cleanly in every measured dimension, but the ordering they fall into is not stable: it reverses with network size and changes again with the metric. The answer to RQ2 is ordinal. The proxy is valid against a theoretical cost metric for every backend whose runtime follows the workload. Its ordering is preserved under substantial error in its own constants, which is what simulator selection requires. With utilisation measured correctly, on this hardware it is largely runtime rescaled, except where a simulator uses several cores. Section 6.5 specifies the physical comparison that would fix its absolute values. RQ3 is answered by a working dashboard and by a design finding: a hardware axis alone can’t represent this comparison, and a backend axis is needed.
643: The comparison uses a single processor-based platform, held constant throughout the campaign (Section 3.4). This is why results are presented as orderings, scaling exponents and rank correlations, not absolute times. The main item of future work in Section 6.5 is extending the same harness to accelerator hardware.
645: Seven contributions were realised. A standardized cross-simulator CPU benchmark suite measured five simulators and eleven executable backends across inference, memory, learning cost and a five-point scalability sweep. It used one machine and one measurement session per experiment, and retained every individual observation. Building on it, a sensitivity analysis of the simulator ordering, realised beyond the original scope, recomputes that ordering at every measured network size and under every measured metric. No comparable published benchmark of these tools reports this. The principal contribution measures how far the ordering moves with size and metric. The rank correlations in Section 4.10 give tau = 0.236 between the orderings at five hundred and ten thousand neurons, reproduced in four sessions. They give tau = +0.418 between the memory and runtime orderings, and tau = 0.236 between the scaling-exponent and runtime orderings. A hardware-agnostic energy proxy was realised as an ordinal metric. It is computed for every run, validated against an analytic synaptic-operation count, and keeps a stable ordering under substantial error in its own constants, the property a selection instrument needs. Physical validation against a power meter is specified in Section 6.5. An interactive dashboard was realised with a design lesson attached: the hardware axis specified in RQ3 cannot express this comparison, and a backend axis is required. An environment and capability probe, also realised beyond the original scope, determines which simulator backends can execute on a given computer. It does so by running a kernel and checking its output, not by consulting a table of supported architectures. It therefore needs no modification to assess hardware released after it was written, and it makes the accelerator extension in Section 6.5 a measurement rather than a survey. Finally, an archived benchmark dataset is released with the thesis and deposited under a citable identifier specified in Section 6.5. It holds per-run records with machine provenance, the study machine's capability profile, the raw replicate observations, and the analysis pipeline that generates every figure and table in Chapter 4.
646: The benchmark suite is a contribution, but the one that matters most is the result it was built to obtain, stated here directly rather than left for the reader to infer. Using a single controlled instrument and measured rank correlations rather than argument, this thesis demonstrates that the ordering of spiking neural network simulators is not a stable quantity. It shifts with the network size at which it is measured, and again with the ranking metric. No published benchmark of these tools reports this about itself. Yet the methodological literature in adjacent fields ⟦C1:[16]⟧, ⟦C2:[17]⟧, ⟦C3:[68]⟧, ⟦C4:[18]⟧ treats reporting it as part of the method, not an extra. Section 4.10 discharges this, and Objective O1 commits to it explicitly for that reason.
647: That different metrics rank things differently is not surprising, and it is not the contribution. The contribution is that the size of the effect has been quantified on one instrument, one machine and one model, with all competing explanations held constant. The movement in the ordering therefore cannot be attributed to differing hardware, network definitions or measurement protocols. These are the usual escape routes when two published benchmarks disagree. What remains is the choice of size and metric, and this study quantifies the value of that choice.
648: The practical consequence for the simulator-selection guidance this thesis aims to provide is that the guidance must be conditional. The dashboard is built for this: readers choose the simulators and view that fit their own situation instead of reading a fixed ranking. On this evidence, that design decision, which Section 3.12 states as an interface decision, is a methodological necessity.
649: The finding's exact claim needs stating, because it is easily overstated in one direction and dismissed in the other. It does not claim that the measurements are unreliable. Coefficients of variation are low throughout, every individual run is retained, and the equivalence check confirms that the simulators produce matching firing rates on the same specification before any timing is compared (Section 6.4). Nor does it say that benchmarking simulators is a waste of time. What it claims is narrower and therefore actionable. An ordering obtained at one network size, under one metric, on one machine is a valid statement about that size, that metric and that machine. Reporting it without those qualifiers turns a valid measurement into an invalid recommendation. More precision is not the answer. This thesis argues for measuring the range a reader might occupy and reporting where the ordering changes, which costs a benchmark one additional analysis.
651: Four features of this study's conduct hold lessons beyond it, each reached by measurement rather than by argument. Section 6.4 records the limits they leave, and Section 6.5 the work that would remove them.
652: First, a benchmark design should include a test of its own stability. The design specified in the proposal fixed one machine and one protocol. That is fine for internal validity, but it gave no way to ask whether the protocol was shaping the result. The mechanism became necessary once the ordering was found to depend on network size, and Experiment 4 was built to provide it. It is now the most transferable part of the work, and it costs one more analysis of data already collected. The lesson is that the test belongs in the design, not in the response to a surprising result. Objective O1 is now written to do just that.
653: A benchmark harness needs testing at more than one scale. Section 4.8 describes the defects found in the measuring instruments and their corrections. The quadratic spike counter is the most instructive. It was invisible at pilot scale, where every configuration completed in seconds, and appeared only when a cost projection to full scale gave an implausible answer. Two practices are adopted here, and both are followed. A projection that seems absurd is treated as evidence about the harness rather than the simulators. And an instrument used only at the scale convenient for testing will be validated at precisely the scale where its defects do not show. The processor-utilisation instrument adds a third practice. Its two defective forms looked plausible and were caught only by testing against loads whose answer is known (Section 4.8). An instrument that has not passed that test should not be trusted with a result.
654: Cost, not accuracy, is the comparable quantity for learning rules, and a design should commit to this in advance rather than discover it. Three of the five simulators use rules that are orders of magnitude less sample-efficient, and more expensive per sample, than the two gradient-based libraries, because they sit at a different point in the taxonomy of ⟦C1:[20]⟧ (Section 3.7). Equalizing the budget would starve the gradient-based simulators or make the plasticity-based ones unaffordable. Section 3.7 fixes cost as the comparable quantity and reports accuracy at a stated budget. Whether the plasticity-based rules converge given the budget they require is a separate question; Section 6.5 states what answering it would need.
655: Choose a measurement platform for what it licenses, not for its power. Fixing one machine lets us read a difference in runtime as a difference between simulators (Section 3.4), whether the machine is modest or, as here, a thirty-two-core laptop. The choice still constrains the threading result, which is a property of this core count, cache topology and scheduler (Section 4.12). Generalizing it would repeat, in the opposite direction, the mistake made by the two-core finding in an earlier draft. On any hardware, a fixed platform delivers orderings, exponents and rank correlations, all dimensionless and transferable, and no conclusion here depends on an absolute time.
656: The fourth lesson concerns the provenance of stored results. Records from superseded attempts and from another machine could silently displace the campaign's own, and at one stage a headline figure was affected. It was found by auditing the stored machine identifier and run_group, not by seeing anything wrong in the figures. Section 4.8 gives the defect and its remedy. The lesson is that an append-only store is the right design for a benchmark, because it makes a partial re-run safe, but the query layer carries the whole burden of deciding what is one campaign, and a layer resolving only on recency will pool hardware without saying so.
658: The empirical scope covers five of the many simulators surveyed in chapter 2, and the conclusions should not be generalized to the rest. One hardware platform was measured, so absolute timings transfer nowhere. What is claimed to transfer is the ordering by scaling exponent, and Experiment 4 is evidence for that claim rather than proof of it.
659: The study measures processor-based execution only, and this thesis does not claim to extend to a GPU. Accelerator execution is a separate campaign, not an omission from this one. The capability paths are implemented and probe-verified, and Section 6.5 specifies the study that would exercise them. The energy proxy is validated ordinally, not physically. Its absolute joule values rest on manufacturer figures not verified for this chassis. The training results are limited by the budget. For the two plasticity-based simulators, they also depend on a presentation window shorter than the reference method uses, as shown in Section 4.8. The workload throughout is a feed-forward network with fixed fan-in (Section 3.13). Training cost is reported as time only: utilisation, memory and energy were not observed during training (Section 4.6).
660: The statistical limits set out in Sections 3.10 and 4.12 apply. They bear most on the Holm-corrected pairwise Welch tests in Section 4.3 for the one backend that fails the Shapiro-Wilk test. However, the omnibus Welch ANOVA and its effect size are reported alongside them and do not depend on every backend being exactly normal. Variability between sessions is reported in Section 4.4.
661: Training results are bounded by the budget. Experiment 2 measures the cost of each simulator's native learning rule, not converged accuracy (Section 3.7). The accuracies in Table 4.4 are outcomes at a budget held constant across every backend, and the full reference configuration, first projected, has since been run in full (Section 4.6). Six of the nine rows are at or below chance, and the rows say so openly. Those rows measure a missing homeostatic mechanism, not a simulator (Section 4.6), and no conclusion in this thesis depends on them. Section 6.5 lays out the converged comparison and the compute it would take.
662: The second limitation concerns thread parallelism. Each simulator was configured as its documentation recommends: the fairest available convention, but not the same as equal resources. Processor utilization ranges from one core to about eight at the reference size, and up to 32 cores across the sweep. Part of what the runtime comparison measures is therefore which simulators use additional cores by default, not which do more work per core. Reporting utilization with each runtime makes the effect visible, and the energy proxy incorporates it directly. But no configuration of this experiment removes it, since forcing each simulator onto a single thread would measure something no practitioner would ever run.
663: A third limitation is that the equivalence check tests agreement on output firing rate and nothing else. Two implementations can produce matching rates while differing in spike timing, in how activity is spread across the population, or in their response to inputs the check does not exercise. The check is sufficient to rule out a fast back-end that solves a substantially easier problem, which is the failure mode it was designed to catch. It is not a proof of numerical equivalence, and this thesis makes no claim of that strength anywhere.
665: The items below are ranked by how much they would strengthen the work. The first is extending the harness to GPU hardware.
666: GPU benchmarking, as a study of capability across machines, comes first. The capability profiles in Appendix B already show the probe giving different verdicts for the same backends on two machines. To establish whether GPU support belongs to the simulators or to the hardware generation, the GPU architecture must be varied across at least three generations. Ideally this includes a non-Nvidia device to exercise the harness's ROCm and Metal paths, which are implemented and probe-verified but not yet used in a measurement campaign. Physical validation of the energy proxy comes next: logging a wall-socket power meter or on-die energy counters during a repeat of the campaign. This would make the ordinal proxy quantitative and complete the contribution claimed in Chapter 1. Extending the scalability sweep beyond the measured ten thousand neurons (discussed below) would show whether the reversal in the measured range is the final ordering. It may instead reverse again at the cortical scale the literature otherwise reports. A full factorial sensitivity design would vary network size and ranking metric together, not one at a time as Experiment 4 does. It would need roughly an order of magnitude more measurement time, or a screening design such as a fractional factorial, and would show whether the two conditions interact or act independently. Comparing learning under the sample budget and presentation window of the reference method (discussed below) would show whether the plasticity-based simulators reach the accuracy of the gradient-based ones once given the budget their rules require. The executed full-budget run now bounds that cost from below. At the 25-millisecond window used here, the full specification cost between 3.5 and 12.2 hours per NEST configuration and between 35.0 and 38.4 hours per Brian2 backend. The reference method's longer window would lengthen every run further. Least valuable by this ranking, but cheapest, is adding adapters for GeNN, Lava and BindsNET to the harness, to test whether the pattern found here generalizes to them.
667: Experiment 2 has since been run at the indicated scale, and Section 4.6 reports its results beside the fixed-budget campaign. The infrastructure already existed and checkpointed across process restarts, so the work needed machine time rather than development. That run settled the cost and one prediction. It did not settle the converged comparison this extension was really for. Two things should come before repeating it. The unsupervised rules should first be given the mechanisms identified in Section 4.6 (lateral inhibition, an adaptive threshold and weight normalization) and validated at a deliberately small sample size. A rule that cannot separate classes at 500 images will not separate them at 60 000, and checking this cheaply avoids spending many hours reaching the same conclusion. That prediction has since been tested from the expensive direction, and it held. The full-scale run was executed without the three mechanisms, and ten times the data moved the plasticity rules by 0.82 to 2.21 percentage points, and none exceeded chance (Section 4.6). Only then does the full-scale run make sense.
668: The memory results suggest a second extension. The per-neuron figures in Section 4.5 come from growth over a sweep that stops at 10 000 neurons. That separates the simulators by an order of magnitude but is far from the scale where NEST's design is supposed to pay off. Extending the sweep until the fixed interpreter cost is negligible for every simulator would turn the selection guide's conditional guidance from an extrapolation into a measurement. It would also test whether the ordering found here holds or inverts a second time.
670: This thesis gives a procedure rather than a winner, which is a practical answer for a researcher choosing a spiking neural network simulator. Start with the network size you want to run. The fastest simulator at 100 neurons is not the fastest at 10,000, and the order flips within that range. Then find out which backend you will actually use, because a single simulator's backends differ more than the simulators do. Finally, check that your hardware can run things before trusting a simulator's advertised acceleration. On a current GPU, the capability probe released with this work found that only one of the four third-party acceleration paths it tested would build and execute. That is a property of the ecosystem worth measuring rather than assuming.
671: The methodological point is narrower and, I think, more durable. A benchmark that reports an ordering has not done its job until it tests whether the ordering comes from the software or from the experiment. The sensitivity analysis in Experiment 4 costs a fraction of the measurement effort of the study it validates. Without it, this thesis would report the same numbers with no way to tell whether they meant anything. More than any single timing, that is what I would want to carry into the next piece of work in this area.
672: There is a version of this thesis that would have been easier to write. It would have run the same five simulators on the same machine, taken the medians, sorted them and published a table with a winner on top. Every number in it would have been right. But the ordering would have been an artifact of the single size and metric that produced it, and nothing in the table would have told the reader so. The table would still have misled. The two theses would not differ in measurement quality. They would differ by one more question, asked of the author's own result rather than anyone else's: would this ordering survive being asked again? Asking it cost one further analysis and materially qualified the conclusion. This work would add that qualification for the next person who benchmarks these tools.
774: No journal articles, conference papers, book chapters or patents have resulted from this thesis at the time of submission. The outputs below are the research artifacts the study released.
776: Artifact 1 - SNN benchmarking suite and dashboard. A Python package implementing one shared network specification across Brian2, NEST, Nengo, snnTorch and SpikingJelly, plus a capability probe, a measurement harness and a web dashboard. It contains the benchmark adapters (benchmarks/), the capability and profiling core (core/), the command-line runner (run.py) and the dashboard application (app.py).
777: Artifact 2 - Measured benchmark dataset. 678 measured runs across 150 conditions on the campaign machine. Each run is stored as a record with simulator version, backend, machine identifier and provenance flag, exported to CSV and to an SQLite database. The database also keeps 462 further condition records, flagged and excluded from every figure. These come from other machines, from superseded or incomplete attempts at this campaign, or from the replication sessions of Section 4.4. Keeping them lets the exclusion in Section 4.8 be audited, not merely asserted.
778: Artifact 3 - Per-machine capability profiles. Machine-readable capability probe output for both experimental machines, recording for each simulator and backend whether it executed and, if not, why.
779: Artifact 4 - Cloud reproduction notebook. A notebook and setup script that provision a clean cloud runtime, install only the packages it is missing and re-run the full benchmark. The campaign can therefore be reproduced without access to the original instance.
783: The suite is a Python package. Each simulator is reached through an adapter implementing one common interface, so the network specification in Table 3.2 is written once and translated per simulator instead of being re-specified five times. The commands below reproduce the Chapter 4 campaign in the order they were run.
786: Two behaviors of the harness matter when reading its output. A simulator with no working backend on the requested device writes no row and prints an explicit skip with a reason. It is never recorded as a zero or a missing value. A run requested on a device that would silently execute elsewhere raises an error rather than storing a mislabelled measurement. An earlier version had this defect, which is documented in Section 4.8.
787: Long runs are resumable. Experiment 2 on the plasticity-based simulators takes hours, and the runner checkpoints inside an epoch rather than at epoch boundaries. It saves the synaptic weights, the adaptive thresholds and, for the gradient-based simulator, the optimiser moments. Saving the optimiser state is deliberate. Restoring weights alone would reset the moment estimates and cause a loss discontinuity at each resume, making the result depend on how often the run was interrupted. For the same reason, accumulated training seconds carry across restarts, so an interrupted run does not report a falsely fast epoch.
791: The capability probe ran before any measurement. It judges usability by allocating a tensor on the target device, running a general matrix multiplication and checking the result numerically. It does not compare the device's compute capability with a list of supported architectures. Each probe runs in its own process, because a mismatched device context can terminate the interpreter in a way that cannot be caught from inside it.
792: Two machines appear in this thesis, and their profiles are given separately. Table B.1 is the machine behind every measurement in Chapter 4: LT68, a laptop with an Intel Core i9-14900HX processor, thirty-two logical cores and no accelerator of any kind. Table B.2 gives the capability profile of a second, GPU-equipped machine, obtained while the probe was being developed. It is kept as an illustration of what the probe reports. No measurement from that machine appears in this thesis, and nothing is pooled across the two.
795: Eight of the fourteen enumerated backends run on the campaign machine. All eight are CPU backends, as the machine has no accelerator.
798: The three unavailable results have different causes, and that difference makes the deferral a finding rather than an excuse. NEST's is a software property and holds on any hardware. Brian2's and Nengo's belong to this architecture and its toolchain, and would very likely resolve on an older card. That is exactly the hypothesis the future work in Section 6.5 is designed to test.
814: This appendix holds the dataset behind Experiment 4. Table D.1 gives the runtime ordering of every measured backend at each network size, the raw material for the size-stability coefficients. Table D.2 gives those coefficients along with the coefficients for the metric comparison. Every value comes from the CPU-corrected session that Chapter 4 reports for Experiments 1 and 3, and can be recomputed from the released database.
820: This appendix reproduces the parts of the benchmark suite an examiner needs to verify that the method in Chapter 3 was implemented as stated. It does not reproduce the full suite: the eleven backend adapters, the Flask/Streamlit dashboard front ends and the SQLite storage layer are released at the repository named in Section 6.5. Four excerpts are given: the adapter interface every simulator implements, the timing driver for the warm-up/measured protocol of Section 3.6, and the energy-proxy calculation of equation (3.8). The fourth is the Kendall’s tau-b implementation behind equation (3.16) and every coefficient reported in Section 4.10.
823: Setup and simulation are timed separately by design (Section 3.6). Folding initialisation cost into simulation time would make a simulator that is slow to set up indistinguishable from one that is genuinely slow to run. An adapter that cannot honour a request raises an error rather than substituting another execution path, which makes the equivalence check in Table 3.2 meaningful.
826: warmup and measured are five and five throughout the canonical campaign (Section 3.6). The five discarded executions absorb one-off costs such as JIT code generation and decoder solving. The five measured executions are stored individually, which section 4.8 and every dispersion statistic in Chapter 4 rely on.
829: This is equation (3.8) exactly: energy is runtime times mean processor utilization as a fraction, times the platform’s thermal design power. It returns nothing, not a number, when utilization was not measured. Utilization is the processor time the measured region consumed divided by its wall time. That processor time covers every thread of the process and the child processes it waited for, read from the kernel's per-process CPU clock. The fifth defect of Section 4.8 describes the two earlier, defective ways of obtaining it.
833: This is the implementation behind equation (3.16) and every tau value reported in Section 4.10, Table 4.8 and Appendix D.2. It runs in the same shared data layer the dashboard reads (Section 3.12). A coefficient in the thesis and the same coefficient in the interface therefore come from one function rather than two that might disagree.
